lessons.title: Applied chords and secondary dominants: a dominant that points somewhere other than home
lessons.explanation: Every chord you have named so far belonged to the key the music was already in. The next idea is the most useful one in chromatic harmony, and it is smaller than its reputation suggests. Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom defines tonicization as treating a chord other than the tonic like a tonic by approaching it with its own dominant, and then defines a secondary dominant as a major triad or dominant seventh chord that resolves to a chord other than the tonic. Open Music Theory describes the same objects as applied chords: chromatic chords borrowed from a temporary key, in which the chord before the slash is the identity of the applied chord within the secondary key and the chord after the slash is the chord being tonicized. Two consequences follow immediately. The first is how you read the label: it goes left to right with the word of replacing the slash, so V/V is five of five, a dominant that points at the dominant. The second is that the sound is already familiar, because V moving to I in a temporary key is the same gesture you have played hundreds of times; the only new element is the accidentals. In C major the diatonic triads are C, D minor, E minor, F, G, A minor and B diminished. Make the second chord major instead of minor and you have D major, spelled D, F sharp, A, which is the dominant of G and therefore V/V. Make the third chord major instead of minor and you have E major, E, G sharp, B, which is V/vi. That is the whole mechanism in one sentence: an applied chord is an altered version of a diatonic chord that shares its root, which is exactly how Open Music Theory introduces it. The alteration is not arbitrary. Almost every applied chord raises a note, and the note it raises is the leading tone of the chord being tonicized, which is why the new chord pulls so hard toward a chord that is not the tonic.
lessons.example: Take an eight-bar phrase in C major at 96 beats per minute, where a beat is 60 divided by 96, which is 0.625 s, and a 4/4 bar is 2.5 s, so the phrase lasts 20.0 s (computed). Suppose the chart reads C, A minor, D, G7, C, A7, D minor, G7. Step one, label what you already know: C is I, A minor is vi, G7 is V7 and D minor is ii. Step two, take the two chords containing notes outside the key and run the procedure given in section 17.4 of Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Stack the chord in thirds to find its root and quality: D major has root D and quality major, so you continue, because the procedure stops immediately if the quality is not major or a major-minor seventh. Then find the note a perfect fifth below the root: a fifth below D is G. Then ask whether that note is the root of a diatonic chord. G is the root of V in C major, so the D major triad is V/V. Step three, apply the same three questions to A7: root A, quality major-minor seventh, a fifth below A is D, and D is the root of ii in C major, so A7 is V7/ii. Step four, read function rather than label. Two chords now point somewhere local: D pushes to G and G pushes to C, while A7 pushes to D minor, so the phrase contains two short moments of direction rather than one long approach home. Step five, test the reading against the bar count. If each symbol lasts one bar, the phrase spends 10.0 s on the tonic and its neighbours, 2.5 s inside the tonicization of V, and 2.5 s inside the tonicization of ii, with the remaining 5.0 s on the closing chords (computed from the 2.5 s bar). Step six, count the chromaticism honestly. Across the five applied dominants available in a major key the notes introduced are C sharp, D sharp, F sharp, G sharp and B flat: five of the twelve pitch classes, which is 41.7 per cent, leaving 58.3 per cent diatonic (computed). That ratio is why a page can look full of accidentals while the music still sounds like it is in C: the chromaticism is local and the diatonic frame is intact.
lessons.question: A progression in C major runs C, E, A minor, D7, G7, C. A learner labels the third chord as iii and the fourth as ii7, arguing that both roots belong to the key. Using the definition of an applied chord and the analysis procedure in section 17.4 of Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom, what are the accurate labels and why?
lessons.answer: E is V/vi and D7 is V7/V, because an E major triad and a D7 chord are altered versions of the diatonic chords that share their roots, and each resolves a fifth downwards to a chord that is not the tonic
lessons.distractor: E is iii and D7 is ii7, because the roots E and D both belong to the key of C major and Roman numerals name roots rather than chord quality
lessons.correction: Root membership is not enough, because the diatonic second and third chords of C major are minor: ii is D, F, A and iii is E, G, B. An E major triad contains G sharp and a D7 chord contains F sharp, neither of which belongs to the key, so both are chromatic chords with the quality that the procedure requires. The section 17.4 test then settles the label: with the quality established as major or major-minor seventh, find the note a perfect fifth below the root, and if that note is the root of a diatonic chord the chord is a secondary dominant. A fifth below E is A, which is the root of vi, so E is V/vi; a fifth below D is G, which is the root of V, so D7 is V7/V. Open Music Theory frames the same chord as an altered version of the diatonic chord sharing its root, so minor ii becomes major II sharp, written V/V.

depth.definitions: A tonicization is the temporary sounding of a non-tonic chord as though it were a tonic. A secondary dominant is a major triad or dominant seventh chord that resolves to a chord other than the tonic, and applied chord is the broader term covering applied dominants and applied leading-tone chords. Slash notation names the applied chord first and the tonicized chord second. Diatonic means belonging to the key at hand; chromatic means containing at least one pitch class outside it. A leading tone is the pitch a semitone below whichever tonic is currently being tonicized, not only the home tonic. Mode mixture, covered in lesson 43, borrows chords from the parallel mode of the same tonic, while tonicization treats another degree as a temporary tonic and imports its dominant. Prerequisites: triad construction and quality from lesson 34, Roman numeral function from lesson 41, fifth relationships from lesson 42, mixture in lesson 43, and chord symbol reading from lesson 61.
depth.mechanism: Applied chords work because one chromatic note changes what the ear predicts. Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom observes that the raised notes generally act as the leading tone to the root of the chord being tonicized; that single semitone creates the same half-step pull that makes a home dominant feel inevitable, but aimed at a different destination. Three limits deserve stating. First, the procedure is a test rather than an oracle: a chord with a chromatic note is not automatically a secondary dominant, which is why the quality check comes first and why the promised resolution has to actually occur. Second, not every degree can be tonicized, since diminished chords such as vii are not tonicized with their own dominant, because a diminished triad cannot serve as a stable temporary tonic. Third, the label describes function and not destiny. A D major chord in C major that never resolves to G is analytically a problem, and the honest annotation says so rather than inventing a resolution that never arrives. Analysis here is an inference from context, quality and resolution, and inference can be revised when the next bars arrive.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two chromatic chords in the same key, because they are easy to confuse and they behave differently. In C major an F minor chord, spelled F, A flat, C, is borrowed from the parallel key of C minor and is a case of mode mixture: the tonic has not moved, and the borrowed chord tends toward the home dominant or a predominant. An A major chord, spelled A, C sharp, E, is a different animal, because C sharp is not a note of C minor at all, so nothing in the parallel mode explains it; instead A is the dominant of D and points at ii. One way to keep them apart is to ask what the chord is trying to become: mixture changes colour while staying home, tonicization changes where home briefly is. A third case shows why identical notes can be labelled two ways. In C minor an F major chord can be V/VII if it resolves to a B flat chord, or IV if it continues toward the dominant, which is exactly the ambiguity the textbook describes when it says the label depends on how the chord functions or progresses rather than on how it is spelled.
depth.mistake: The most common error is relabelling by root only, so D7 in C major becomes ii7 and E major becomes III. Root membership feels like an argument until you check quality: the diatonic second and third chords are minor, so a D major chord and an E major triad contain pitch classes that do not belong to the key at all. The diagnostic takes ten seconds and is mechanical: name the root, name the quality, then ask which chord lies a perfect fifth below that root and whether it is diatonic. A second error is concluding that the piece has modulated. It has not; tonicization is local, and if the key really moved, a cadence would confirm the new key, which is the subject of the next lesson. A third error is to reach for a new hand shape the moment a sharp appears, before deciding where the chord goes, which converts an analysis problem into a fingering problem and usually produces the wrong chord in the right place.
depth.application: Task, at the desk and then with one instrument, in a single 20-minute sitting with a two-minute warm-up and the instrument at a comfortable volume. Choose eight bars of any progression you can read or already play, in a key you know. Write the root and quality of every chord in a column. Then run the three-question test on each chromatic chord and write the resulting slash label beside it. Finally, list the destination of every applied chord and mark which destinations are themselves unaltered diatonic chords. Model response for C, A minor, D, G7, C, A7, D minor, G7: roots C, A, D, G, C, A, D, G; qualities major, minor, major, dominant seventh, major, dominant seventh, minor, dominant seventh; two chords fail the diatonic quality test, so D is V/V and A7 is V7/ii; destinations are V and ii respectively, both diatonic. Self-review rubric: one point for naming quality before drawing any conclusion, one for applying the perfect-fifth test rather than guessing from shape, one for stating the destination of each applied chord, one for a written sentence naming a chord you had been mislabelling. Warm up before playing, keep the session under 25 minutes, and stop if a hand or wrist aches; discomfort during a repeated passage is a signal to change the setup rather than a threshold to push through.
depth.summary: An applied chord is a chromatic chord that makes another chord sound briefly like home. The three-question test - root, quality, then which note lies a perfect fifth below the root and whether that note is diatonic - turns a page of accidentals into a list of short journeys, each with a destination. The idea transfers directly to charts, to transcriptions and to the chord symbols you will type into a project, and it sets up the harder question that follows: whether the music has merely visited another key or has actually moved there.

lessons.title: Tonicisation or modulation? Two tests that separate a visit from a move, and the pivot chord between keys
lessons.explanation: A tonicization and a modulation can look identical for four bars and then turn out to be different things, so the distinction has to be made by evidence rather than by impression. The evidence is duration plus confirmation, and both textbooks give tests rather than definitions to memorise. Open Music Theory puts it plainly: modulation involves a longer-term change of tonic, in contrast to the temporary nature of tonicization, and it offers two pieces of advice for finding one. Cadences establish keys, so identify the cadences before you begin the analysis, and a repeated accidental in a passage is a sign of a possible modulation, so when you see a consistent accidental, look for the cadence that establishes the key it implies. Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom makes the same point operationally: a modulation to a new key requires an eventual cadence to confirm that new key, and that cadence will often use a full cadential formula of pre-dominant, cadential six-four, dominant and tonic. It also admits the ambiguity honestly: that formula establishes a key more strongly than a plain V to I authentic cadence, which means there will be genuine uncertainty between a tonicization and a short modulation ending in an authentic cadence, especially where the harmonic rhythm is fast. So the practical answer to the question in the title is not a rule but a search: find the cadence in the suspected new key, and check whether its dominant was approached by its own predominant. If it was, you are looking at a modulation; if the chromatic chord resolves and the music returns at once to the old tonic, you are looking at a tonicization. Once the key has changed, the device that makes the change sound inevitable is the pivot chord, which Open Music Theory defines as a single chord that is diatonic in both the home key and the new key, written with the two Roman numerals stacked, the upper one for the old key and the lower one for the new key.
lessons.example: Work a modulation from G major to D major by hand, because the arithmetic is small and the method is the point. Step one, list the diatonic triads of both keys. In G major they are G, A minor, B minor, C, D, E minor and F sharp diminished. In D major they are D, E minor, F sharp minor, G, A, B minor and C sharp diminished. Step two, find the chords with the same root and the same quality in both lists, since Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom specifies that in a diatonic common chord modulation the pivot chords must be diatonic in both keys. Comparing the lists, G, B minor, D and E minor qualify, so four of the seven triads are shared, which is 57.1 per cent (computed). Step three, choose the pivot by function rather than by convenience, because both sources agree on a ranking: the pivot should not have dominant function in the new key, the best choices are predominant in both keys, and the second best option is a tonic in the old key becoming a predominant in the new. Our four candidates split as follows. G is I in G and IV in D, a tonic becoming a predominant, which is the second-best kind. E minor is vi in G and ii in D, predominant in both keys, which is the best kind. B minor is iii in G and vi in D, two weak predominants. D is V in G and I in D, which involves the dominant and is exactly the kind of pivot both sources warn against because the change can sound abrupt. So the choice is E minor or G. Step four, write the two labels stacked, old above new, and check that the dominant of D arrives shortly afterwards with its own predominant in front of it. Step five, put a number on the shape of the change so it can be planned rather than hoped for. At 84 beats per minute a beat is 0.714 s and a 4/4 bar is 2.857 s, so a four-bar approach to the pivot is 11.429 s and an eight-bar phrase is 22.857 s (computed). The pivot therefore needs to arrive early enough that D major has time to be confirmed by a cadence rather than merely touched in passing.
lessons.question: A passage begins in B flat major, introduces an F sharp diminished seventh chord that resolves to a G minor chord in bar four, and then continues with tonic and predominant chords of B flat major for the rest of the phrase. Using the tests in this lesson, what is the accurate analysis and what evidence decides it?
lessons.answer: It is a tonicization rather than a modulation, because the phrase confirms B flat major with its own cadential material, so G minor has only been made to sound briefly like a tonic
lessons.distractor: It is a modulation to G minor, because a seventh chord built on the raised fourth degree cannot be explained in B flat major and a new key must therefore have begun
lessons.correction: A chromatic chord proves that something non-diatonic has happened; it does not prove that the key changed. Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom states that a modulation to a new key requires an eventual cadence to confirm that new key, and Open Music Theory advises identifying cadences before analysing anything, since cadences are what establish keys. Here the phrase closes in B flat major, so nothing confirms G minor, and the repeated-accidentals test also fails because the F sharp does not persist. The F sharp diminished seventh is functioning as an applied leading-tone chord pointing at vi - F sharp is a semitone below G - which is the applied-leading-tone counterpart of the applied dominants in lesson 71.

depth.definitions: Modulation is a longer-term change of tonic, sometimes called a key change. Tonicization is the temporary sounding of a non-tonic chord as tonic. A pivot or common chord is a single chord diatonic in both keys, labelled with the old key's Roman numeral above the new key's. A direct or phrase modulation moves to the new key abruptly, usually at a phrase boundary. Closely related keys have key signatures one degree sharper or flatter than the starting key, and any major or minor key has five of them, including its relative major or minor. A cadential formula is the pre-dominant, cadential six-four, dominant, tonic pattern that confirms a new key. Prerequisites: the applied-chord test of lesson 71, Roman numeral function from lesson 41, circle of fifths reasoning from lesson 42, key signatures from lesson 33, and phrase and cadence awareness from lesson 46.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms work on different time scales. The local mechanism is the applied chord, which creates a half-step pull toward a chord that is not the tonic. The structural mechanism is the cadence, which is the only thing that can install a new tonic, because a key is not a collection of notes but a hierarchy of stability, and hierarchy is established by arrival rather than by vocabulary. That is why the textbook formula for confirming a key is a cadential progression rather than one chord, and why the sources warn that a short passage ending in a plain authentic cadence can honestly be read either way: the confirmation is there, but its strength is arguable. Two further limits matter. Mode mixture and modal progressions can produce chromatically altered chords that are not modulations at all, so a chromaticism is a prompt to look further rather than a conclusion. And popular music often changes key with no pivot, moving directly up a whole tone or to the relative minor at a section boundary, in which case the honest analysis names the direct change and says that the smoothness came from the phrase boundary rather than from voice leading.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the same two keys connected two ways. In the first version, G major moves to D major by way of E minor, which is vi in G and ii in D: the chord sounds entirely ordinary in the old key, the bass moves stepwise, and a listener notices nothing until the cadence in D arrives. In the second version the band plays a G major bar and then a D major bar at the start of the chorus with no pivot at all. Both are modulations by the test of eventual cadence in the new key, but only the first is a common-chord modulation; the second is a direct or phrase modulation, which Open Music Theory notes tends to occur at phrase boundaries and which is analysed simply by naming the new key and continuing. A third contrast closes the loop with lesson 71: if the second version returned to G major after two bars, the label would change again from modulation to tonicization of V, because the only evidence that would be missing is the confirmation.
depth.mistake: The most frequent mistake is treating any accidental as proof of modulation, which converts an applied chord into a key change and then produces an analysis of the following bars in the wrong key. The diagnostic is the cadence search, performed before any chord is named, because the sources put cadence identification first for exactly this reason. A second mistake is choosing a pivot chord because it is easy to play rather than because of its function; a pivot with dominant function in the new key sounds abrupt, which is why the textbooks advise against it, so an analysis resting on one is likely to be wrong. A third mistake is writing the two Roman numerals without saying which belongs to which key, which makes the annotation unreadable to anyone else and useless to yourself six months later. A fourth is assuming that recurring accidentals must mean a modulation without checking that they add up to a plausible key signature; the modulation chapter's cue list asks you to add recurring accidentals to the key signature, treat raised notes as the likely leading tone and lowered notes as the likely fourth degree, and remember that accidentals which cancel out indicate tonicizations or chromatic non-chord tones rather than a new key.
depth.application: Task in two parts, about 25 minutes with a break, with an instrument needed only for part two. Part one, on paper: take a piece with a suspected key change, mark the phrase endings first and label the cadence at each one, identify the new key from the cadence, and only then find the pivot by working backwards. The recommended strategy is to analyse in the old key until it stops making sense, then back up a chord and try that as the pivot. Write the two labels stacked and state the function of each. Part two, at the instrument: play the four-bar approach to the pivot at 84 beats per minute, then play the same four bars with the pivot removed and a direct change in its place, and note which version hides the change and which announces it. Model response: phrase one ends with a half cadence in G major at bar four and phrase two ends with an authentic cadence in D major at bar eight, so the keys are G and D and the shared triads are G, B minor, D and E minor; the chosen pivot is E minor, vi in the old key and ii in the new, predominant in both; at 84 beats per minute the four-bar approach is 11.429 s and the pivot sits in bar three of eight. Self-review rubric: one point for finding cadences before naming chords, one for a pivot justified by function in both keys, one for correctly stacked notation, one for a listening note comparing the pivot version with the direct version. Keep the sitting under half an hour, warm up before playing, and keep the monitoring level low enough to hear the room; if a phrase makes your wrist or forearm ache, stop and reset your hand position before continuing.
depth.summary: A key change is a claim that requires evidence, and the evidence is a cadence in the new key. Cadences first, accidentals second, pivot third: that order is the method, and it also tells you what to write when the case is genuinely ambiguous, which the sources concede it can be. The pivot chord, chosen for function rather than for convenience, is what makes the change sound inevitable, and the same reasoning reverses cleanly to explain why a fleeting chromatic chord is not a modulation at all.

lessons.title: Diatonic modes: the same seven pitches around a different centre, and the one note that supplies the colour
lessons.explanation: Major and natural minor are not two collections of notes; they are two ways of treating one collection. The modes are the rest of that family, and Open Music Theory supplies both the definition and the shortcut. The modes are understood as rotations of the major scale, with no range requirements, but with the concept of a pitch-class centre or tonic, and the same chapter gives the parallel relationships in a form you can use while playing, because each mode is exactly one note away from a scale you already know. Ionian is identical to major. Aeolian is identical to natural minor, with no raised leading tone. Mixolydian is like major with a lowered seventh degree. Lydian is like major with a raised fourth. Dorian is like natural minor with a raised sixth. Phrygian is like natural minor with a lowered second. The relative view is the other half of the same idea, and it is what makes the keyboard so convenient: within the white-note collection, Ionian starts on C, Dorian on D, Phrygian on E, Lydian on F, Mixolydian on G and Aeolian on A. Both descriptions are correct and they answer different questions. The relative view tells you which notes to play. The parallel view tells you why the mode sounds different from the major or minor scale sharing its tonic, because it shows you the single altered degree. The popular-music chapter names that degree precisely: each mode has exactly one pitch that is inflected relative to its major or minor counterpart, and that pitch is called the colour note of the mode. If one sentence has to carry out of this lesson, it is that a mode is a collection plus a centre, and its character comes from a single degree being in an unexpected place.
lessons.example: Take D and build three modes on it, because keeping the tonic fixed is what makes the colour audible. Step one, write the relative version. D Dorian is the white notes starting on D: D, E, F, G, A, B, C. Step two, write the parallel version using the rule that Dorian is natural minor with a raised sixth. D natural minor, which is D Aeolian, is D, E, F, G, A, B flat, C. Raise the sixth degree from B flat to B and you have D, E, F, G, A, B, C, which is exactly the white-note collection. The two descriptions agree, which is a useful check that neither rule has been misapplied. Step three, locate the colour note: D Dorian differs from D Aeolian on precisely one scale degree, the sixth, which is a semitone higher than in the minor. Now compare D Mixolydian with D Ionian. D Ionian is the major scale on D, containing F sharp and C sharp; D Mixolydian is that scale with a lowered seventh, so C sharp becomes C natural, and the colour note is the seventh. D Phrygian is D Aeolian with a lowered second degree, so E becomes E flat, giving D, E flat, F, G, A, B flat, C. Across these modes on the same tonic, each differs from the nearest familiar scale by exactly one note, and each of those changes is a single semitone (computed from the spellings). Step four, count the material: any of these modes uses seven of the twelve pitch classes, which is 58.3 per cent, and the modal character comes from which seven and, more importantly, which one is the centre (computed). Step five, test the centre rather than assuming it, because the collection is identical to a major or minor scale and the same seven notes can be read two ways. The analysis chapter offers a starting heuristic for deciding: the first, last, loudest, longest maxim, attributed there to Cohn after Harrison, which says that pitches dominating in those four ways are the ones most likely to be heard as the centre. Step six, allow for exceptions honestly. The same chapter notes that modal music may contain chromatic notes, so not every pitch used needs to belong to the collection, and it asks the reader how many exceptions would be too many.
lessons.question: A guitarist plays the same six-note figure in the same order twice, once starting and ending on A and once starting and ending on C, and reports that the first sounds settled and minor while the second sounds unresolved. Using the modal definitions in this lesson, what is the accurate explanation?
lessons.answer: The two passages use the same collection with different centres, so the first reads as Aeolian with A as tonic and the second as Ionian read from C, and perceived stability follows which pitch functions as the centre
lessons.distractor: The two passages must contain different notes, because a mode is defined by its own fixed set of pitches, so the second passage has necessarily replaced some notes in order to sound major
lessons.correction: Open Music Theory defines the modes in two ways and both make the identity of the collection clear: relatively, as the white notes starting on different degrees, and in modern usage as rotations of the major scale with a pitch-class centre or tonic. Aeolian is identical to natural minor, so reading the same collection from A gives a minor third above the tonic and a settled minor quality, while reading it from C gives a major third above C. The collection is unchanged and the centre has moved, which is why the two passages sound different while containing the same pitches. The same chapter also warns that modal music may contain chromatic notes, so pitch content and mode are related questions rather than the same question.

depth.definitions: A mode is a collection of pitches together with a referential centre, called a final in the church-modal tradition and a tonic or pitch-class centre in modern usage. A diatonic mode uses the seven pitches of the diatonic collection. Ionian and Aeolian are identical to major and to natural minor respectively. The colour note of a mode is the single pitch inflected relative to its major or minor counterpart. A rotation is the same collection read from a different starting pitch, and there are seven of them. Modal mixture, by contrast, means borrowing a chord from the parallel mode while remaining in a major or minor key. Church, white-note or Gregorian modes are classified by collection, final, the relationships of other pitches to that final, and range. Prerequisites: major and minor scales and key signatures from lesson 33, scale-degree names, the pentatonic vocabulary of lesson 66, and the tonic-versus-centre reasoning of lesson 41.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism is that perceived stability depends on distance and placement, not on membership alone. A collection cannot by itself say where home is, because the same seven pitches can support seven different centres, and what supplies the centre is a combination of emphasis: the pitch that begins phrases, ends them, is repeated, sits on strong beats, or occupies the top of the contour. That is why the analysis literature recommends the first, last, loudest, longest test as a starting point and presents it as a way of arguing for a centre rather than of proving one. Three limits deserve statement. First, a modal progression can appear inside an otherwise tonal song, so a single modal schema does not require the whole piece to be modal; the popular-music chapter says as much about modal schemas. Second, the characteristic effect of a mode depends on the chords placed underneath it, not on the scale alone, so a Dorian passage that never sounds its raised sixth degree distinctly will be heard as ordinary minor. Third, the relative and parallel definitions are both standard, and confusing them produces real errors, which the transposition comparison below demonstrates.
depth.secondExample: Transpose the idea and the two definitions separate, which is a good test of understanding. D Dorian is the white-note collection, so the relative and parallel descriptions coincide and it is easy to conclude that Dorian simply is the white notes. Move the tonic to A and the illusion breaks. A Dorian is not the white notes from A, because the white notes from A give A natural minor, which is A Aeolian with F natural. A Dorian requires F sharp instead, so the collection becomes A, B, C, D, E, F sharp, G, which carries one sharp, exactly as the parallel rule predicts, since Dorian is natural minor with a raised sixth. The analysis chapter makes the same point about transposition, noting that while early modes are usually presented in white-note transposition, twentieth-century music just as easily places Dorian on E or Phrygian on D. A second contrast concerns the colour note in practice. Play a four-bar loop alternating D minor and G major and you have the Dorian shuttle, where the raised sixth, B natural, is what stops the passage sounding like ordinary D minor. Change the second chord to G minor and you have not merely altered one chord's quality; you have removed the mode.
depth.mistake: The most common misconception is that modes are simply scales to practise, so the learner plays seven patterns from a book without changing the chords underneath and concludes that the modes sound identical. In that exercise they do sound identical, because a collection without a centre and without harmonic support has no mode. The diagnostic is to fix one tonic and move one note at a time: play D Aeolian, then D Dorian, then D Mixolydian, and name which degree moved each time; if you cannot hear the difference, change the harmony rather than drilling more patterns. A second mistake is believing that Dorian means the white notes, which is true only when the tonic is D, and being surprised when a Dorian passage on A needs F sharp. A third is treating a modal progression as an error because it contains a chord that is not diatonic in major or minor, such as a flat seven major chord in a Mixolydian passage; the published schema lists show such chords as the substance of the style rather than as exceptions to a rule.
depth.application: Task, one sitting of 20 to 25 minutes with a two-minute warm-up and the instrument at a comfortable volume. Choose a tonic and write the scales you will compare: your reference major or minor, then Dorian, Mixolydian and Phrygian on the same tonic. For each, write the note that differs from the reference and the direction of the semitone. On the keyboard play each as a single line in one octave with shoulders relaxed and wrists straight; on the guitar play each on one string so the fret numbers are visible. Then play a two-chord loop under one mode and stop there: for example D minor to G major under D Dorian, and D minor to G minor under D Aeolian, and write which one you would use for a section you are writing. Model response: reference D Aeolian, D E F G A B flat C; D Dorian raises the sixth from B flat to B; D Mixolydian lowers the seventh of D major from C sharp to C; D Phrygian lowers the second from E to E flat; on the keyboard Dorian on D is all white keys, which is why it is the easiest first mode to see and the easiest to misunderstand; under D Dorian the loop D minor to G major sounds open and unresolved, whereas D minor to G minor sounds like ordinary minor. Self-review rubric: one point for naming the changed degree and its direction, one for a physically relaxed single-string or single-position fingering, one for a chord loop that actually sounds the difference, one for a written sentence about which mode you will use and what it changes in your piece. Warm up before playing, keep the sitting short with a break, and never raise the monitor level to hear a detail you could hear by turning the room noise down.
depth.summary: A mode is a collection plus a centre, and the centre decides the sound while the colour note decides the flavour. Keeping the tonic fixed and moving one note is the fastest way to hear the difference, and the same reasoning transfers to writing modal sections, to choosing chords under a modal melody, and to reading the modal progressions listed among the popular-music schemas.

visual.title: Modes as one collection with seven possible centres - reasoning sequence
visual.description: One seven-note collection, seven candidate tonics, and a single altered degree that gives each mode its colour.
steps: Write the collection once: the seven pitch classes of the diatonic set, which is 58.3 per cent of the twelve.
Choose the centre and name the mode from it: the same notes read from D give Dorian, from G give Mixolydian, from A give Aeolian.

lessons.title: Cadences: naming how a phrase ends, and why V-to-not-I is the more honest description
lessons.explanation: A cadence is the punctuation of music, and naming cadences is how you find out where phrases end, which in turn is how you find out what key you are in. Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom defines a cadence as a harmonic arrival point, a harmonic moment of stasis, and compares it to a comma or a period in written language: the ear gets a moment to process a short passage of music, then the music continues. That source then gives four basic cadences, and they are worth learning as four chords pairs rather than as four adjectives. An authentic cadence is a phrase ending with V to I. A plagal cadence is a phrase ending with IV to I. A deceptive cadence is a phrase ending with V to vi. A half cadence is a phrase ending on V. Open Music Theory refines the first of these in a way that matters for analysis: authentic cadences involve V to I, they are perfect when both harmonies are in root position and the tonic scale degree is in the soprano over tonic, and if either condition is not met the authentic cadence is imperfect. That is the whole vocabulary needed for this lesson, but two refinements in the sources keep it honest. First, a half cadence is defined as the progression x to V, where x is any of a variety of harmonies, so the label describes where the phrase arrives rather than the route. Second, the deceptive cadence is defined by what did not happen: the textbook states that because a deceptive cadence means V did not go to I, the description V to not-I is technically more accurate than V to vi, which is simply the most common realisation of it. A cadence therefore tells you that a phrase has ended and how strongly, and it simultaneously tells you the key, because endings are where keys are confirmed.
lessons.example: Take an eight-bar period in C major at 100 beats per minute, where a beat is 0.6 s and a 4/4 bar is 2.4 s, so the whole period lasts 19.2 s (computed). Suppose the first four bars close with the chords D minor, G and the phrase stops on G, and the second four bars close with F, G and then C. Step one, label the two endings. The first phrase ends on G with no arrival at the tonic, so it is a half cadence. The second phrase moves V to I, so it is an authentic cadence. Step two, decide how strong the authentic cadence is, using both conditions Open Music Theory gives. Are both chords in root position, and is the tonic scale degree in the soprano over the final chord? If the soprano lands on E, the third of the chord, the cadence is imperfect even though it is a genuine arrival; if the soprano lands on C with G in the bass under it, the cadence is perfect. Step three, count the time each ending occupies. A V to I pair occupying the last two beats takes 1.2 s, which is half of a 2.4 s bar and 6.25 per cent of the 19.2 s period (computed). Two beats is enough to be heard as an arrival precisely because the preceding harmonic rhythm has been slower. Step four, check how the four basic cadence types distribute across this scheme. Two of the four types end on the tonic, namely the authentic and the plagal; one ends on a tonic substitute, the deceptive cadence ending on vi; and one does not close at all, the half cadence ending on V. So calling half the vocabulary closing and half of it not closing is a fair summary, and it explains why the OMT phrase chapter treats a phrase as a thought whose goal is a perfect authentic, imperfect authentic or half cadence (computed from the four definitions). Step five, use the cadences to find the key, because this is the practical payoff. If you know the first phrase half-cadences on G and the second authentic-cadences on C, you have located C major without counting a single accidental, which is the method lesson 72 relied on.
lessons.question: A four-bar phrase in C major ends with the chords G then A minor, and a learner annotates it as an imperfect authentic cadence on the grounds that the final chord is not the tonic in root position. What is the accurate label, and what wording correction do the sources require?
lessons.answer: It is a deceptive cadence, and the more accurate description is that V moved to not-I, with V to vi being the most common realisation of that description rather than its definition
lessons.distractor: It is an imperfect authentic cadence, because an authentic cadence becomes imperfect whenever the final harmony is not the tonic in root position
lessons.correction: An authentic cadence is V to I, and Open Music Theory describes it as perfect when both harmonies are in root position and the tonic scale degree is in the soprano over tonic, and imperfect when either condition fails. The condition being tested is therefore the position and the soprano note, not the identity of the final chord, so an imperfect authentic cadence still ends on the tonic. A move from V to vi does not end on the tonic at all, which places it in a different category: Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom lists V to vi as a deceptive cadence and then states that because a deceptive cadence means V did not go to I, V to not-I is technically a more correct description than V to vi. The practical difference is that an imperfect authentic cadence closes the phrase while a deceptive cadence deliberately declines to, so a performer needs to know which one is in front of them.

depth.definitions: A cadence is a harmonic arrival point, a moment of relative stasis at the end of a phrase. An authentic cadence is V to I, perfect when both harmonies are in root position and the tonic scale degree is in the soprano over tonic, otherwise imperfect. A plagal cadence is IV to I. A deceptive cadence is V to vi in its most common form, more strictly described as V to not-I. A half cadence is a phrase ending on V, reached from any of a variety of harmonies. The soprano is the upper voice, and root position means the root of the chord is in the bass. An incomplete chord contains a root and a third but no fifth, while a chord with only root and fifth is labelled with a 5 after the root, as in B5, a familiar shape in rock. Prerequisites: triads and their inversions from lesson 34, Roman numerals from lesson 41, functional categories from lesson 41 and lesson 75, and the phrase definition from lesson 46.
depth.mechanism: Cadences are heard because closure is created by motion from instability to stability, and the strength of that closure can be graded. The dominant is unstable because it contains the leading tone, a semitone below the tonic, and in a seventh chord it also contains a tritone; resolving either of those into the tonic produces the most directed close available in tonal music, which is why the authentic cadence is the default ending. Three consequences follow that analysis has to respect. First, strength is not the same as type: a V to I with the third in the soprano is still an authentic cadence and still closes the phrase, but it closes it more softly, which is why the sources distinguish perfect from imperfect rather than treating one as correct and the other as deficient. Second, a half cadence works by withholding resolution: the phrase stops on the chord that wants to continue, which in a two-phrase period sets up the answering phrase. Third, the label is a classification of an event in context, so it can be revised; the harmonic-analysis method in the next lesson begins by identifying phrase endings by ear precisely because the ear's first guess is an input rather than a verdict. Finally, not every style closes phrases with cadences at all: in popular music a phrase may be completed by a melodic length or a line of lyric, which is why cadence-hunting in pop sometimes returns fewer results than harmony-hunting does.
depth.secondExample: Hold the chords constant and change only the destination, which isolates the label from the material. In C major, G to C is an authentic cadence; G to A minor is deceptive; F to C is plagal; and a phrase that stops on G without arriving anywhere is a half cadence. Four phrases, one shared chord in three of them, four different structural meanings. A second contrast concerns the same cadence type heard at two strength levels. End a phrase with G in the bass and C above it in root position with the tonic in the soprano, and the listener experiences a full stop; end it with the third chord of C in the bass, which is first inversion, or with the third or fifth in the soprano, and the phrase still closes but the arrival is softened, which is why the perfect condition is stated as two requirements rather than one. A third case is specific to rock and pop. Where a phrase ends on a chord containing only a root and a fifth, the sources instruct you to label it with a 5 after the root, as in B5, and where it contains root and third but no fifth it is called an incomplete chord; both are common at the end of loud sections, and neither is a misprint.
depth.mistake: The most damaging misconception is treating the words as verdicts on quality, so a learner hears imperfect as wrong and deceptive as a mistake by the performer. Both labels describe structure: an imperfect authentic cadence is a real close with a softer landing, and a deceptive cadence is a composer's deliberate refusal to close, which is exactly why it is useful in a song that needs to continue after a chorus. The diagnostic is to write the Roman numerals under the two chords and ask whether the phrase has arrived at the tonic; if it has, the cadence is authentic and the only remaining question is how strong. A second mistake is calling any V that goes somewhere other than I deceptive regardless of what happens next, when the definition depends on the phrase ending at that point; V moving to vi in the middle of a phrase is simply a motion within the phrase. A third mistake is assuming every phrase must have a cadence, since popular-music phrases can be closed by lyric or melodic completion. A fourth is inferring the bass from a chord symbol; unless a slash is written, the symbol says nothing about which note is lowest, which is precisely the information the perfect-and-imperfect test requires.
depth.application: Task in two parts, about 25 minutes with a short break. Part one, on paper: take one piece you can read a chord chart for, mark every phrase ending, and label each with one of the four types; then state for each authentic cadence whether it is perfect or imperfect and give the reason. Part two, at the instrument with the volume comfortable and hands warmed up: play all four endings over a two-bar loop in a key you know, once each, and write one sentence per ending describing what the listener would expect to happen next. Model response for C major: ending on G leaves the phrase open and demands a continuation; G to C closes it, and with C in the bass and the tonic in the soprano it is perfect; F to C is a softer close associated with the plagal motion; G to A minor refuses the close and can be used to postpone a chorus. At 100 beats per minute each bar is 2.4 s, so a two-beat cadence occupies 1.2 s, which is the amount of time the listener has to register the arrival. Self-review rubric: one point for labelling all four types correctly from the chord pairs, one for a perfect-or-imperfect judgement supported by the bass and the soprano rather than by feel, one for correctly declining to call a mid-phrase V to vi a deceptive cadence, one for describing what each ending makes the listener expect. Keep the session under half an hour, take a short break in the middle, and stop if the hand or wrist aches rather than playing through it.
depth.summary: A cadence is where a phrase arrives, and the four basic types are defined by their final two events: V to I closes strongly, IV to I closes softly, V to something other than I declines to close, and a phrase left standing on V does not close at all. Naming cadences does double duty, since the same labels locate phrases and confirm keys, and the graded strength of the authentic cadence is what lets an analysis say how firmly a section has landed rather than merely that it has.

visual.title: Four ways a phrase can end, and how strongly - reasoning sequence
visual.description: One key, one shared dominant, four destinations, and a strength test applied to the only ending that truly closes.
steps: Write the four chord pairs before listening to anything: V to I authentic, IV to I plagal, V to vi deceptive in its usual form, x to V half.
Sort them by whether the phrase ends on the tonic: only the authentic and the plagal cadences do, so only two of the four close on the home chord.

lessons.title: Analyse a whole section: phrase model, strong predominant, cadence, and a key you can defend
lessons.explanation: Analysis stops being guesswork the moment the order of operations is fixed, and Open Music Theory supplies that order. Its harmonic-analysis chapter instructs you to identify phrase endings by listening, then provide a harmonic analysis of the cadence at each ending, then back up from the cadence to find the strong predominant that leads into it, and only then analyse from the beginning of the phrase, using your knowledge of tonic prolongations to guess what is happening and then verifying the guess against the notes in the chords. The chapter adds the labels that make the result readable: for each phrase you get one set of functions, a tonic beginning, a predominant, a dominant, and a tonic ending, and phrases almost always progress through them in that direction rather than backwards. The other chapters in the same book supply the pieces those labels need. Functional categories are three: tonic, which in Western classical music is I alone; predominant, split into strong predominants such as IV and ii and weak predominants such as iii and vi; and dominant, which is V and the leading-tone chord. A schema is the parallel tool for popular music: publicly listed stock progressions with names and Roman numeral patterns, including the twelve-bar blues, the plagal IV to I, doo-wop as I, vi, IV, V, the singer-songwriter pattern vi, IV, I, V, hopscotch as IV, V, vi, I, the lament as i, flat VII, flat VI, V, and the circle-of-fifths pattern vi, ii, V, I. Schemas are prototypes that remain recognisable while being altered, which makes them fast to recognise and dangerous to rely on exclusively. Finally the form chapter supplies section vocabulary, because in verse-chorus songs the sections are not distinguished by harmony alone: verses are lyric-variant and often narrative, they tend to begin on the tonic, and a prechorus is recognised above all by a gain in energy, with fragmentation and an acceleration of harmonic rhythm.
lessons.example: Analyse a sixteen-bar verse in C major at 96 beats per minute, where a beat is 0.625 s, a bar is 2.5 s, a four-bar phrase is 10.0 s and the whole section is 40.0 s (computed). The chords are C, A minor, F, G7 in bars one to four; C, A minor, D7, G7 in five to eight; C, E minor, F, F minor in nine to twelve; and C, G7, C, C in thirteen to sixteen. Step one, find the phrase endings by listening rather than by counting, then check by counting: the harmonic rhythm is one chord per bar and the section falls into four four-bar phrases, which is the common length the phrase chapter describes. Step two, analyse the cadence at each ending. Phrase one ends on G7, which is a half cadence. Phrase two also ends on G7, another half cadence, but this time the dominant was prepared by D7, which is V7/V from lesson 71 and therefore a strong approach to the dominant. Phrase three ends on F minor, which is not a cadence but a colour change, so the phrase is left open and the arrival comes later. Phrase four ends G7 to C, an authentic cadence, and whether it is perfect or imperfect depends on the bass and the soprano at the final chord, per lesson 74. Step three, label the functions. Phrase one is tonic beginning, predominant on F, dominant on G7, and no tonic ending because it half-cadences. Phrase two runs tonic beginning, predominant, and a dominant preceded by its own applied dominant, again without a tonic ending. Phrase three begins on the tonic and then moves to E minor, a weak predominant, F as a strong predominant, and F minor as mixture borrowed from C minor; it also has no tonic ending. Phrase four is the only phrase carrying the full set, tonic beginning, predominant absent, dominant, and tonic ending. Step four, go back to the beginning and verify each guess against the actual notes, which is the step beginners skip. A minor in bar two is vi, a tonic prolongation rather than a predominant; E minor in bar ten is iii, a weak predominant; F minor in bar twelve contains A flat, which is not in C major, which is what identifies it as mixture rather than an error. Step five, name the schema if one is present. The opening C, A minor, F, G is the doo-wop pattern I, vi, IV, V, and naming it explains why phrase one sounds complete while ending on the dominant. Step six, write the two-sentence conclusion, which is the deliverable: the section is in C major, confirmed by one authentic cadence in bar fifteen and undermined by nothing, with three phrases left open and one chromatic chord described as mixture.
lessons.question: A learner analyses a 32-bar pop section by naming every chord as it appears from left to right, produces a page of Roman numerals, and finds that the labels stop making sense around bar 20. Using the harmonic-analysis method in this lesson, what should have been done first, and what does the breakdown most likely indicate?
lessons.answer: Phrase endings and their cadences should have been identified first, because cadences are what establish keys; the breakdown at bar 20 most likely marks a modulation whose new key would have been found from the cadence before the labels were attempted
lessons.distractor: The key signature of the section should have been assumed to be fixed, because a 32-bar pop section does not change key and the labels must therefore have been transcribed incorrectly
lessons.correction: The method is ordered deliberately: identify phrase endings by listening, analyse the cadence at each ending, look for the strong predominant leading into the cadence, and only then analyse from the beginning. That order makes a change of tonic visible, because a cadence is what establishes a new key and a modulation is a longer-term change of tonic. The assumption that a section cannot change key is contradicted by the same material: direct modulations occurring at phrase boundaries are described as an ordinary device, and popular music frequently changes key without any pivot at section boundaries. A page of labels in the wrong key is the predictable result of naming chords before locating the cadences that decide which key each label belongs to.

depth.definitions: The phrase model is the typical order and flow of harmonic functions within a phrase. The four function labels are tonic beginning, predominant, dominant and tonic ending, applied once per phrase in that direction. Tonic function belongs to I alone; strong predominants are IV and ii; weak predominants are iii and vi; dominant function belongs to V and the leading-tone chord. A tonic prolongation is material that extends the tonic without leaving it, typically a motion to vi or to a first-inversion tonic. A harmonic schema is a stock progression recurring across many pop songs with a name and a Roman numeral pattern, and schemas are prototypes that can be altered while remaining recognisable. Harmonic rhythm is how long each chord lasts. Verse-chorus form divides the title lyrics, the most memorable music and the main narrative between two core sections, with prechorus, bridge and postchorus as other possible sections. Prerequisites: functional analysis from lesson 41, applied chords from lesson 71, modulation from lesson 72, cadences from lesson 74, and form marking from lessons 46 and 47.
depth.mechanism: The order of operations works because of what each step can and cannot establish. Listening for endings uses the ear's ability to hear arrival, which is more reliable than reading for boundary markers, since a boundary is usually marked by several parameters changing at once. Analysing the cadence next fixes the key, because arrival is what installs a tonic. Backing up to find the predominant is efficient because predominant-to-dominant is the standard approach, so the chord before the cadence is heavily constrained. Analysing from the start last is safe because the local functions are now known, so the remaining work is to assign prolongations and to flag chromatic chords as applied or borrowed. Two honest limits apply. Schema recognition is fast but can be wrong: a passage resembling doo-wop may be altered enough that its function has changed, and the chapter's own framing is that schemas are prototypes with common variations. And in popular music the section label may depend on energy, lyric variance and instrumentation rather than on harmony, so two sections with identical chords can still be a verse and a postchorus.
depth.secondExample: Analyse the same eight bars in the two orders and compare the output. Left to right, the passage C, A minor, D7, G7, C, A7, D minor, G7 yields a list in which a reader cannot tell which chords are structural and which are decoration, and the two applied dominants sit unremarked among six ordinary chords. Right to left, the same bars produce a phrase ending on G7, a strong predominant on D7 identified as V7/V, a tonic beginning on C, a prolongation through vi, a second phrase with V7/ii applied to ii, and one clear conclusion: the passage is in C major with two applied dominants, one half cadence, and no modulation. The second order costs a minute more and produces a defensible sentence. A second contrast concerns the two tools. A schema tells you what a progression resembles in a corpus; a phrase model tells you what a phrase is doing here; a good analysis may cite both, but only the phrase model can explain why an altered version of a familiar loop still closes on the dominant.
depth.mistake: The commonest failure is producing a list of chord names and calling it an analysis, which answers what the chords are and never answers what they are doing or where the phrase ends. The diagnostic is to cover the Roman numerals and read only your own function labels: if several bars have no label and no stated reason, the analysis has become a transcription. A second mistake is relying on a schema name as a substitute for functional reasoning, so a passage labelled doo-wop is assumed to be closed because that is what the schema usually does. A third is assuming that a repeated four-chord loop means there is only one section, when the form chapter shows that sections are distinguished by lyric variance, energy and texture as well as by harmony, with the prechorus recognised chiefly by an energy gain and an acceleration of harmonic rhythm. A fourth is treating a chromatic chord as an error, which sends the learner looking for a misprint instead of testing the applied-chord questions from lesson 71 and the mixture questions from lesson 43.
depth.application: Task, one sitting of 30 minutes, mostly at the desk with an instrument used for the listening checks and warmed up first. Choose any section of sixteen bars or longer. Write nothing for the first pass; listen twice and mark with a pencil where you hear endings. Then label each cadence, then find the predominant before each cadence, and only then work forward from the beginning assigning tonic beginnings and prolongations. Finish with three written sentences: the key and the cadence that confirms it, the two chords that are chromatic and what each is doing, and the one thing you would have got wrong if you had analysed left to right. Model response in the style of the worked example: the section is in C major, confirmed by the authentic cadence at bar fifteen; D7 in bar seven is V7/V and F minor in bar twelve is mixture from the parallel minor; analysing left to right I would have labelled D7 as ii7 and F minor as an error, and would have missed that phrases one to three never close. Self-review rubric: one point for phrase endings marked before any chord was named, one for cadences labelled with reasons rather than guesses, one for identifying every chromatic chord as applied or as mixture, one for the closing sentence naming what the wrong order would have produced. Warm up before playing, keep the sitting to half an hour with a short break, keep the listening level moderate, and stop if the hand or wrist aches.
depth.summary: A section analysis is an argument, and the argument has an order: endings first, cadences second, predominants third, and the beginning last, with one set of function labels per phrase. The same method absorbs applied chords, mixture, schemas and section vocabulary without turning into a list, and its output is a claim about a key that another musician can check.
