visual.title: From a page of chords to a defended analysis - reasoning sequence
visual.description: Four passes over one sixteen-bar section, ordered so that the key is established before any chord is named.
steps: Pass one, listen only: mark phrase endings with a pencil and do not name a single chord.
Pass two, label the cadences at those endings: half cadence on G7 in phrases one and two, authentic cadence in phrase four.
Pass three, back up from each cadence to find the strong predominant, which is what exposes D7 as V7/V preparing the dominant.
Pass four, work forward from the start assigning tonic beginnings and prolongations, then test every chromatic chord: F minor contains A flat and is mixture.
State the conclusion as a sentence with evidence: the section is in C major, at 96 beats per minute each four-bar phrase lasts 10.0 s, and only the fourth phrase carries a tonic ending.

questions.prompt: A rehearsal chart in F major reads F, D7, G minor, C7, F, one chord per bar, at 96 beats per minute. A player says the D7 leaves the key and wants to know what to call it. Computed from that tempo, how long is the progression, and which label is correct for the D7?
questions.answer: The progression lasts 12.5 s, and D7 is V7/ii, because a fifth below D is G and G is the root of ii in F major
questions.distractor: The progression lasts 12.5 s, and D7 is VI7, because a major chord built on the sixth degree is standard practice in a major key
questions.correction: At 96 beats per minute a beat is 0.625 s, so a 4/4 bar is 2.5 s and five bars are 12.5 s. The diatonic triads of F major are F, G minor, A minor, B flat, C, D minor and E diminished, so D major, which contains F sharp, is not among them; the root-name label VI7 fails because the diatonic sixth chord in a major key is minor. The applied-chord test then settles it: the quality is major-minor seventh, and a perfect fifth below D is G, which is the root of ii, so the chord is V7/ii.

questions.prompt: Two versions of the same passage begin in A major. Both introduce an A7 chord in bars three and four resolving to D. In the first version the music returns to A major for eight bars; in the second it stays in D and closes with an authentic cadence in D. What is A7 doing, and what evidence separates the two versions? At 84 beats per minute, how long do those eight bars of the first version last?
questions.answer: A7 is V7/IV in both versions, and the difference is confirmation: the first version tonicizes IV and returns home, while the second modulates to D because a cadence establishes the new key, and eight bars at 84 beats per minute last 22.857 s
questions.distractor: A7 is a diatonic dominant seventh in A major in both versions, and the difference is simply the length of the passage, which at 84 beats per minute is 22.857 s for eight bars
questions.correction: A major contains G sharp, so an A7 chord with G natural is chromatic: Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom notes that in the major mode the only secondary dominant with a lowered chromaticism is V7/IV, and that the lowered note functions as the fourth degree of the chord being tonicized, which here is G natural as the fourth degree of D. So A7 is V7/IV. Whether the passage is a tonicization or a modulation is decided by evidence rather than by length: a modulation requires an eventual cadence to confirm the new key, so the first version, returning to A major with no cadence in D, is a tonicization, while the second is a modulation. Eight bars at 84 beats per minute, where a bar is 2.857 s, is 22.857 s.

questions.prompt: A learner writes a passage using only white notes, begins and ends phrases on D, and labels it D major, planning to fix the seventh degree afterwards. Using the modal definitions and the colour-note idea, what is the accurate description and what would D major require?
questions.answer: It is D Dorian, because the white notes centred on D give a minor third and a raised sixth; D major would require both F sharp and C sharp, which is two changes rather than one
questions.distractor: It is D major with a lowered seventh, since naming D as the tonic settles the third and the only remaining alteration is the seventh degree
questions.correction: The white notes read from D are D, E, F, G, A, B, C, which is D natural minor with the sixth degree raised, and that is Dorian as the parallel definitions state it: Dorian is like natural minor with a raised sixth. The third above D in that collection is F natural, so the mode is minor in quality and the label D major is wrong at the third, not merely at the seventh. D major requires F sharp and C sharp, so two notes change rather than one, and Dorian is not simply major with a lowered seventh - that description belongs to Mixolydian.

questions.prompt: Two four-bar phrases in C major end differently. The first ends with G7 followed by a C triad with C in the bass and the tonic scale degree in the soprano. The second ends with G7 followed by a C triad in first inversion with the third of the chord in the soprano. How should each ending be labelled, and how long does each final two-chord pair occupy at 100 beats per minute?
questions.answer: Both are authentic cadences; the first is perfect because both chords are in root position and the tonic is in the soprano over tonic, and the second is imperfect because the final chord is inverted and the soprano note is not the tonic; each pair lasts 1.2 s
questions.distractor: The first is a perfect authentic cadence and the second is a plagal cadence, because a first-inversion tonic at the end loses its dominant and behaves like IV to I; each pair lasts 1.2 s
questions.correction: An authentic cadence is V to I, and the perfect condition has two parts: both harmonies in root position, and the tonic scale degree in the soprano over the final chord. The second phrase fails both parts, so it is an imperfect authentic cadence, which still closes the phrase; it is not a plagal cadence, because the preceding chord is G, the dominant, not F, the subdominant. At 100 beats per minute a beat is 0.6 s, so a bar of four beats is 2.4 s and the final two beats of that bar are 1.2 s, which is the window a listener has to hear the arrival.

questions.prompt: A sixteen-bar section in C major at 96 beats per minute is made of four four-bar phrases: C, A minor, F, G7; then C, A minor, D7, G7; then C, E minor, F, F minor; then C, G7, C, C. A learner is asked to label the function of each phrase and the duration of each. What is the accurate labelling, and how long is one phrase?
questions.answer: The first three phrases each begin on the tonic and end without a tonic ending, since phrases one and two close on G7 and phrase three closes on F minor, so only the fourth phrase carries the full set of tonic beginning through predominant to dominant to tonic ending; each four-bar phrase lasts 10.0 s
questions.distractor: Every phrase must carry the full set of tonic beginning, predominant, dominant and tonic ending because the phrase model requires all four functions in a phrase, and each four-bar phrase lasts 10.0 s
questions.correction: The phrase model describes a trajectory rather than a requirement that all four labels appear: a phrase needs at least tonic and dominant function to have direction, and the tonic ending label belongs to a phrase that actually closes on the tonic. Here phrases one and two end on G7, which is a half cadence, and phrase three ends on F minor, which is mixture from the parallel minor rather than a cadence, so none of them has a tonic ending. Only the fourth phrase, with G7 to C, carries the complete set. At 96 beats per minute a bar is 2.5 s, so four bars are 10.0 s and the whole section is 40.0 s.

units.title: Putting the analysis into the hands and the project: applied chords on guitar and keyboard, modal colour, harmony as editable note data, and one proven key change

lessons.title: Play a secondary dominant: the shape you already own, and two voices that move one semitone
lessons.explanation: Analysis delivers a chord; the hands still have to deliver it, and in the friendly keys the physical work is far smaller than the label suggests. An applied chord is an altered version of the diatonic chord with which it shares a root, so in C major the chord that tonicizes V is D major, which is the open D shape a beginner learns in the first month, and the chord that tonicizes vi is E major, which is the open E shape for the same reason. Where the shape is not already under your fingers, one fretboard rule covers every case: one fret is one semitone, so a movable shape shifted up one fret rises a semitone, and a chord belonging to a key a whole tone away is the same shape two frets higher. On the keyboard the equivalent is that a triad moved by a semitone is the same hand shape with every finger shifted by one key, and that shift will often take a finger onto a black key: D major is D, F sharp, A, and F sharp is the black key between F and G. What turns four correct notes into music is voice leading, and this is where an applied dominant earns its reputation. D7 in C major is D, F sharp, A, C, and it resolves to G7, which is G, B, D, F. Two of the four voices move by a single semitone: the seventh of D7, which is C, falls to B, the third of G7, and the third of D7, which is F sharp, falls to F, the seventh of G7. D is common to both chords and can be held or repeated, and if you are playing four voices, A descends a minor third to F to complete the second chord. That is the physical instruction in full, and it explains why the applied dominant sounds inevitable rather than bolted on: the chromatic note is not scenery, it is a voice with one semitone to travel.
lessons.example: Build the progression on the instrument with a tempo ladder, and count the changeover rather than the chords. The progression is C, then D7, then G7, then C, one chord per bar, and the object of the exercise is the move from D7 to G7. Step one, isolate the smallest version on the keyboard: play F sharp and C together in the right hand, which are the third and the seventh of D7, then move both fingers down one key to F and B, which are the seventh and the third of G7. Both voices move a semitone in the same direction, the finger pattern does not change and the hand does not travel. Step two, do the same on the guitar if you play one: F sharp on the fourth string at the fourth fret and C on the second string at the first fret, then move both down a semitone to F on the fourth string at the third fret and B on the open second string. Step three, set the ladder. At 60 beats per minute a 4/4 bar lasts 4.0 s, so the hand has 4.0 s to make the change; at 68 the bar is 3.529 s, at 76 it is 3.158 s, at 84 it is 2.857 s, at 92 it is 2.609 s and at 96 it is 2.5 s (computed). The fastest rung is 1.667 times quicker than the slowest, so the ladder covers a wide range in six steps. Step four, set the budget: play ten four-bar passes at each rung and move up only when at least nine of the ten contain no late or missed change. Step five, spend the session where the error is. If the change is late at 84 but clean at 76, the extra two rungs do not need to be visited at all, and the honest record is the rung at which the change became unreliable. Step six, warm up first, because the physical evidence here is unusually clear. A published survey of guitar players reported that 53 per cent of 105 respondents described injury related to practice, worked out at one injury for every 2,381 practice hours, and found that failure to warm up was the only variable statistically associated with increased risk of injury. At 30 minutes a day, which is 182.5 hours a year, 2,381 hours is about 13 years; at two hours a day it is about 3.3 years (computed). A beginner will not approach that exposure quickly, and the finding worth acting on today is the warm-up, not the total.
lessons.question: A guitarist playing in F major is told that the chord before the B flat chord is an applied dominant and assumes she must learn an unfamiliar shape high on the neck. Using the construction of applied chords and the fretboard rule, what is the accurate answer, and what is the keyboard equivalent?
lessons.answer: The chord is F7, which is the F shape already held with the fourth-string finger moved from the third fret to the first to give E flat, and on the keyboard the same event is one finger shifting down a semitone
lessons.distractor: The chord is B flat major transposed up a whole tone, which requires a movable barre shape because applied dominants always lie outside the key, and on the keyboard it is a triad shifted up a whole tone
lessons.correction: In F major the chord being tonicized is IV, which is B flat, and the chord that tonicizes it is the tonic turned into a dominant seventh: F7, spelled F, A, C, E flat. Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom notes that in the major mode the only secondary dominant with a lowered chromaticism is V7/IV, and that the lowered note acts as the fourth degree of the chord being tonicized, which here is E flat as the fourth degree of B flat. On the guitar that E flat is the fourth string at the first fret, so the existing F shape needs one finger moved two frets rather than a new shape discovered. The barre route is the correct answer only when the applied chord's root is not already under the hand.

depth.definitions: A chord shape is a fixed fingering; a movable or barre shape is one that can be slid along the neck so that each fret of movement is one semitone. Voice leading is the motion of individual parts between chords. Guide tones are the third and the seventh of a chord, the two notes that define its quality and direction. A common tone is a pitch shared by two consecutive chords. A shell voicing is a reduced voicing containing only the guide tones. An applied or secondary dominant is a major triad or dominant seventh resolving to a chord other than the tonic. Prerequisites: applied-chord construction from lesson 71, guide tones as presented in lesson 66, chord changing and hand position from lesson 35, and the tempo-ladder method from lesson 65.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms make the physical work small, and both are worth naming because they generalise. The first is root-sharing: because an applied chord is an altered version of a diatonic chord with the same root, any key whose applied dominant happens to be a major chord already in your vocabulary costs nothing to play, which is why a guitarist in D major can produce both E7 before A and the open B7 shape before E minor without learning anything new. The second is semitone voice leading: the two notes that make a dominant seventh chromatic relative to its target - the third and the seventh - typically move by semitone when the applied dominant resolves, so the change can be executed by sliding fingers rather than by rebuilding a chord. Two limits should be stated. A movable shape concentrates the load across a barre, which is more hand work than an open shape and is the reason the movable route should be practised in short bursts. And the analytic identity of a chord says nothing about register: V7/ii played in first inversion in the middle of the keyboard is the same harmony as the same chord played low on a guitar, so the label constrains the notes and not the voicing.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two ways of playing the same two bars on the keyboard. In the first, the left hand plays a full D7 in root position and the right hand plays a full D, F sharp, A, C, then both hands jump to a root-position G7; every voice departs, the thumb has to travel a fifth, and the chromatic half-step that gives the progression its pull is buried among larger motions. In the second, the left hand keeps D and the right hand plays only the guide tones, F sharp and C, then slides down one key to F and B while the left hand moves D to G; the two semitone motions are now the most prominent events in the texture, which is why the second version sounds more purposeful with fewer notes. A third contrast is the guitar case where the shape is genuinely not owned. In the key of C, a player comfortable with open chords will find D7 and the open E shape immediately; a player whose vocabulary is only barre shapes will find them as movable shapes and will then discover that the change is heavier in the hand, which is a technique problem rather than a theory problem.
depth.mistake: The most common misconception is that an applied chord must require an unfamiliar grip, so the learner hunts for a barre before checking whether the chord is already in the hand; the diagnostic is to name the root of the applied chord and ask which chord of the home key shares that root, because the alteration is usually a single note. A second mistake is playing applied dominants as isolated block chords with all voices jumping, which removes the two semitone motions that make the resolution sound intentional and turns the progression into a sequence of separate events. A third is practising the change at performance tempo before it is secure, which stores the late change rather than the change; the ladder exists to keep the erroneous version off the instrument. A fourth, specific to instrument teaching, is skipping the warm-up because the session is short, which is precisely the wrong trade: in the published survey of guitar practice injuries, failure to warm up was the only variable statistically associated with increased risk.
depth.application: Task, one session of 20 to 25 minutes with the instrument at a comfortable volume. Before playing, check the setup: sit or stand with shoulders relaxed and level, wrists straight rather than bent, the fretting elbow slightly bent, the instrument positioned so the hand does not have to reach, and on the keyboard the chair set so the forearms are roughly level with the keys with both feet supported. Then warm up for two minutes with slow, quiet movements well inside your comfortable range. Write the ladder 60, 68, 76, 84, 92, 96 with the bar duration beside each, play the D7 to G7 change for ten passes at each rung, and record the number of changes that were late or missed. Finish with one written sentence naming the rung at which the change became unreliable and one naming the smallest version of the change you used. Model response: bar durations 4.0, 3.529, 3.158, 2.857, 2.609 and 2.5 s; ten passes at each rung up to 84 clean with two late changes at 84; the change became unreliable at 84 beats per minute; the smallest version was the two guide tones alone, F sharp and C moving to F and B, which fixed the hand before the full chord was added. Self-review rubric: one point for a documented setup and warm-up, one for a complete ladder with computed bar durations, one for an honest count of late changes rather than an impression, one for naming the smallest useful version of the change. Stop the session if a hand, wrist or forearm aches; a repeated physical task that hurts is information about the setup, not about your endurance.
depth.summary: Playing an applied dominant is usually a smaller physical job than its label suggests, because the chord shares a root with one you already play and because its resolution moves two voices by a semitone. Isolate the guide tones, slide rather than rebuild, climb a ladder with a written error budget, and warm up before the first repetition, since the warm-up is the one practice variable a beginner can act on immediately.

readings.title: [109] Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom (Robert Hutchinson) - Section 17.3 Secondary Dominants in Major and Minor
readings.note: Read the whole short section. It states that both major triads and major-minor seventh chords can serve as secondary dominants, that the raised notes generally act as the leading tone to the root of the chord being tonicized, and that in the major mode the only secondary dominant with a lowered chromaticism is V7/IV, where the lowered note acts as the fourth degree of the chord being tonicized. That last statement is the theory behind the F7 example in this lesson, and the section also explains why diminished chords cannot be tonicized.

readings.title: [110] Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom (Robert Hutchinson) - Section 31.7 Jazz Chord Voicings, including Subsection 31.7.1 Guide Tones
readings.note: Read the section introduction and Subsection 31.7.1 on guide tones. It defines guide tones as the third and seventh of a chord and shows that in circle-of-fifths progressions the guide tones move by step, which is the reason this lesson's smallest version of the change is two notes that slide one semitone. Read it before building the two-note shell so the reduction is understood as a voicing decision rather than a compromise.

readings.title: [111] University of Iowa Head and Neck Protocols - Guitar Playing, Part 1: Health Considerations
readings.note: Read the Overview and Definitions sections, which report that roughly 16 million people in the United States began learning guitar in the two years before October 2021, that 53 per cent of 105 surveyed guitar players described injury related to practice, calculated as one injury per 2,381 hours of practice, and that failure to warm up was the only variable statistically associated with increased risk of injury. It also defines playing-related musculoskeletal disorders as symptoms that interfere with playing at the level you are used to. This is education about prevention and practice habits, not a diagnosis of your hands or a treatment plan. The page last carried a 2024 date when checked during authoring.

visual.title: From label to fingers: an applied dominant in two voices - reasoning sequence
visual.description: One chromatic chord reduced to its guide tones, then executed as a one-semitone slide, then placed on a tempo ladder with an error budget.
steps: Name the chord from the analysis: in C major the applied dominant before G is D7, spelled D, F sharp, A, C.
Reduce it to the two guide tones that carry the pull: F sharp as the third and C as the seventh.
Move both voices down one semitone to F and B, which are the seventh and third of G7, so the hand shape does not change.
Set the ladder with the bar durations beside it: 4.0 s at 60 beats per minute down to 2.5 s at 96, a ratio of 1.667 between the slowest and fastest rung.
Require nine clean changes out of ten before climbing, and warm up for two minutes first, since failure to warm up was the one variable associated with practice injury in the survey cited here.

lessons.title: Modal colour in the hands: one shape per mode, and the single fret or key that changes the sound
lessons.explanation: A mode becomes real when the hands can produce it and the ear can hear it, and there are two routes into the hands that teach different things. The first is the single-string route on the guitar, which exposes the intervals because every note is visible as a fret number. The second string of a guitar tuned to standard pitch is the D string, and if you play it open and then at frets 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 10 you get D, E, F, G, A, B, C, which is D Dorian exactly; play the same notes but move the sixth degree from fret 9 down to fret 8 and you get D, E, F, G, A, B flat, C, which is D Aeolian. One fret is the difference between the two modes, which is the colour-note idea in physical form. Play the third string, the G string, open and then at frets 2, 4, 5, 7, 9 and 10 and you get G, A, B, C, D, E, F, which is G Mixolydian; move the seventh degree from fret 10 up to fret 11 and you have G major, so here one fret separates Mixolydian from Ionian. On the keyboard the same idea appears as a count of black keys rather than frets: D Dorian uses no black keys at all, D Aeolian uses one, B flat, D Mixolydian uses one, F sharp, and D Ionian uses two, F sharp and C sharp (computed from the spellings). That count is worth noticing because it is a property of the tonic rather than of the mode, and it is the reason a beginner who treats Dorian as the white keys will be surprised the first time Dorian is asked for on A, where F sharp becomes necessary. Once the fingers have the notes, the mode has to be made audible, and that is a matter of emphasis and harmony rather than of collection. A mode is a collection together with a centre; the analysis chapter suggests the first, last, loudest, longest test for judging which pitch is functioning as the centre, and the schema chapter supplies progressions that carry a mode, including the Dorian shuttle from i to IV, the Mixolydian subtonic shuttle from I to flat VII, and the Aeolian shuttle of i, flat VII, flat VI, flat VII.
lessons.example: Build the demonstration on one string so the arithmetic is visible, then move it to the keyboard and to chords. Step one, play D Dorian on the fourth string: open, then frets 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, which gives D, E, F, G, A, B, C. Step two, play D Aeolian on the same string: open, then frets 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, which gives D, E, F, G, A, B flat, C. The two modes differ at exactly one position, the sixth degree, and the distance is one fret, which is one semitone. Step three, do the same for the Mixolydian and Ionian pair on the third string: open, then frets 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 gives G Mixolydian, G, A, B, C, D, E, F, and moving the seventh from fret 10 to fret 11 gives G Ionian, G, A, B, C, D, E, F sharp. Step four, repeat the whole exercise at the keyboard and count black keys instead of frets: D Dorian takes none, D Aeolian takes one, D Mixolydian takes one, D Ionian takes two. Step five, make the centre audible. Play a two-bar loop at 76 beats per minute, where a bar is 3.158 s and the loop is 6.316 s, using D minor to G major for the Dorian shuttle, then change the second chord to G minor and play D minor to G minor for a plain Aeolian i to iv. Same tonic, one chord changed, and the mode changes with it. Step six, test which note is doing the work by playing a melody that lands on B natural, the raised sixth, on the first beat of the bar, then the same melody landing on B flat: the difference in character between the two passes is the colour note, and hearing it is the point of the exercise. Step seven, put the physical work on a ladder. At 60 beats per minute the two-bar loop lasts 8.0 s, at 68 it lasts 7.059 s, at 76 it lasts 6.316 s, at 84 it lasts 5.714 s, at 92 it lasts 5.217 s and at 100 it lasts 4.8 s (computed), so the loop still has room to breathe at the fastest rung, which is what a modal demonstration needs because the character lives in the space between notes.
lessons.question: A learner practises D Dorian on the keyboard by playing all the white keys from D upward and back down, then writes a four-bar passage using those notes and is told the mode is not audible. Using the colour-note and modal-schema material, what is the diagnosis and what is the fix?
lessons.answer: The collection is correct but the centre is not audible: emphasising D as the last and strongest note, exposing the raised sixth B natural, and supporting the passage with a Dorian shuttle such as D minor to G major are what make the mode heard
lessons.distractor: The collection is wrong, because Dorian requires a raised fourth degree rather than a raised sixth, so a different set of notes must be built from D
lessons.correction: D Dorian is D natural minor with a raised sixth, so the white keys read from D are exactly right, and the raised fourth is the colour note of Lydian rather than of Dorian. What is missing is everything that makes a centre audible. The analysis chapter defines a mode as a collection together with a referential final or tonic, recommends the first, last, loudest, longest test for deciding which pitch is functioning as the centre, and notes that modal music may even include pitches outside the collection, which shows that membership is not what defines the mode. The schema chapter names Dorian progressions as the Dorian shuttle of i to IV, which in D is D minor to G major. A passage that wanders through the correct notes without a harmonic frame and without a prominent raised sixth will be heard as the parent major collection, or as nothing in particular.

depth.definitions: A mode is a collection of pitches with a referential centre. A colour note is the single pitch inflected relative to the major or minor scale on the same tonic. A shuttle, in the schema literature, is a two-chord oscillation, such as Dorian i to IV. A modal schema is a stock modal progression that can appear without the whole song being modal. Position playing on the guitar means playing a scale within a fret span rather than along one string. The single-string route is used here because it makes each interval a visible fret distance. Prerequisites: the modal definitions and colour notes of lesson 73, the pentatonic vocabulary of lesson 66, movable shapes and the capo from lesson 54, and the tempo-ladder method of lesson 65.
depth.mechanism: The physical mechanism is that a mode's character is carried by very few frets. Compare the pairs used here: Dorian and Aeolian on D differ by one fret because the sixth degree moves a semitone, Mixolydian and Ionian on G differ by one fret because the seventh degree moves a semitone, and the same is true of Phrygian against Aeolian at the second degree and Lydian against Ionian at the fourth. The auditory mechanism is that the ear assigns a centre, and it assigns it from emphasis rather than from membership, which is why a passage can be correct note for note and still be heard in the parent key. Two limits follow. A mode practised without chords will usually sound undifferentiated, because nothing in the accompaniment argues for the centre. And a keyboard habit built on white keys can quietly teach that Dorian means the white notes, which is true only when the tonic is D; transposing the same mode to A requires F sharp, and the analysis chapter says as much when it notes that modes can be transposed and that Dorian need not sit on D. The guitar has a parallel hazard: position patterns make the scale fast to play and hide the location of the tonic inside the shape.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the same mode delivered two ways on the guitar. The single-string route plays D Dorian along the fourth string and makes every interval legible, which is why it is the route used to demonstrate that Aeolian is one fret away, but it is slow and awkward for real playing. The position route plays the same notes inside a four-fret span with several strings, which is fast and musical but leaves the tonic implicit, so a learner can play the pattern fluently and still not know where home is. Doing both, one after the other, is the fastest way to convert a pattern into a mode. A second contrast is harmonic. Take the identical D Dorian melody and place D minor and G major underneath it, then place D minor and G minor underneath it: the melody has not changed and the mode has, because the second version replaces the characteristic chord with the plain minor one. A third contrast concerns transposition: A Dorian needs one black key, F sharp, while D Dorian needs none, so a learner who has internalised Dorian as a keyboard geography rather than a set of relationships will be surprised at the first transposition.
depth.mistake: The most common misconception is that learning a mode means learning a scale pattern, so the learner practises seven shapes, hears seven similar sounds, and concludes that modes are an academic distinction. The diagnostic is to keep the tonic and the chords fixed and move one note, as the paired fingerings in this lesson do; if the character changes, the mode is real and the pattern was hiding it, and if it does not change, the harmony underneath is not supporting the mode. A second mistake is assuming the white keys are Dorian, which is true only for D, and being surprised when a Dorian passage on A needs F sharp. A third is to treat the raised sixth of Dorian as an ornamental note to be touched and left rather than as the note that defines the sound, which throws away the only evidence the ear has. A fourth is physical: scale practice done with a tense hand, a collapsed wrist or a raised shoulder stores the tension along with the notes, which is why two minutes of warm-up and a session under half an hour with a break matter more in this lesson than in most.
depth.application: Task, one session of 20 to 25 minutes with a two-minute warm-up, the instrument at a comfortable volume and the setup checked first: relaxed shoulders, straight wrists, elbows slightly bent, keyboard chair set so the forearms are level with the keys and both feet supported. On the guitar, play one mode along one string, then the same mode in a position, then say out loud which degree is the colour note. On the keyboard, play the same mode and count how many black keys it uses. Then play a two-bar loop with the modal chord and the plain chord, and write two sentences: which chord made the mode audible, and which note you will land on at the end of your next phrase. Finish with a short ladder so the demonstration has a tempo record: 60, 68, 76, 84, 92, 100, with the loop duration written beside each as 8.0, 7.059, 6.316, 5.714, 5.217 and 4.8 s. Model response: D Dorian on the fourth string is open then frets 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, and D Aeolian changes only fret 9 to fret 8; the colour note is the sixth degree, B natural, which is the raised sixth; the loop D minor to G major made it audible, while D minor to G minor did not; at 84 beats per minute the loop is 5.714 s and that is the rung where I stopped playing accurately. Self-review rubric: one point for producing the mode on the instrument without a chart, one for naming the colour note and the degree it occupies, one for a chord loop that hears the difference rather than merely stating it, one for a written tempo record with the computed loop durations. Warm up, break the session up, and if the hand or wrist aches, change the setup rather than playing through it.
depth.summary: Modes live one fret apart and one chord apart: the frets supply the notes, the colour note supplies the character, and the chord underneath supplies the centre. Practising a mode along one string, then in a position, then over its own shuttle converts a pattern into a sound you can reproduce on request, and the same method transfers to the modal progressions you will meet in other people's songs.

visual.title: One mode, one string, one fret of difference - reasoning sequence
visual.description: A mode shown as fret numbers along a single string, then as black-key counts on the keyboard, then heard through its own chord loop.
steps: Play the fourth string open and then at frets 2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10 to hear D Dorian as D, E, F, G, A, B, C.
Change only the sixth degree, moving fret 9 to fret 8, and hear D Aeolian: one fret is the entire difference between the two modes.
Play the third string open and then at frets 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 for G Mixolydian, then move fret 10 to fret 11 for G Ionian, again a single fret.

Make the centre audible with a chord loop: D minor to G major for the Dorian shuttle at 76 beats per minute, where a two-bar loop lasts 6.316 s.

lessons.title: Program the harmony: note data is not sound, and the piano roll is where the analysis becomes editable
lessons.explanation: Everything you have analysed so far can be typed into a project, and the reason it is worth typing rather than playing is that a project stores something different from a recording. The FL Studio manual makes the distinction twice and both places are worth knowing. The MIDI Out plugin page states that MIDI Out does not make any sound of its own and acts as a MIDI controller sending standard MIDI messages to internal plugins or external hardware. The piano roll page states that note data can be entered manually with the editing tools or recorded in from live MIDI controllers, and then edited to fix mistakes or make changes. Alongside those, the Transport Panel's recording filter separates Notes, which record note data from a keyboard or drum pads, from Audio, which records sound. Put together, the software is telling you that a keyboard performance can enter the project as information about which note, when and how hard, and that information is editable per note; a guitar or a voice enters as a waveform, and editing it means processing sound. That single distinction decides what is cheap and what is expensive in every later stage, and it matters most for exactly the work of this level, because a chord progression built from analysis is data. You can move the D7 from bar seven to bar eight, change one note of it, re-voice it in another octave, change its velocity, or swap the instrument entirely without touching a waveform. Two tools in the piano roll support this work directly. The Chord Progression Tool, opened from the piano roll's Tools menu, offers chord progressions with a Conventional to Adventurous slider, allows the tonic note and the scale to be changed, and offers to snap the piano roll to a scale and root note so that later notes stay in harmony with the progression. The chord stamp tool places a chord of a chosen type at the clicked pitch and time, following the current snap and scale settings. And the piano roll's scale setting requires a scale to be chosen before a root note is available, after which scale snapping, highlighting and shading follow that root. None of these tools analyses anything, which is why the analysis work of unit one has to come first: a generator can give you chords that sound plausible, but only you can say that the seventh bar contains V7/V and why.
lessons.example: Build eight bars of harmony as note data, with the analysis decided before the mouse is touched. The target is a progression in C major: C, A minor, D7, G7, F, F minor, C, G7. Step one, write the functions by hand: I, vi, V7/V, V7, IV, iv by mixture, I, V7. Step two, open the piano roll for a polyphonic instrument, because a monophonic synth cannot play a chord, and set the scale and root so that highlighting marks the C major collection. Step three, enter the first four chords with the chord stamp, then check the D7 by hand rather than trusting it: it must contain F sharp, which is the chromatic note that makes it V7/V, and if the stamped chord came out as D minor you have a ii7 and the analysis has been silently changed. Step four, do the same for F minor in bar six, whose identifying note is A flat, and confirm that the mixture chord is present rather than an F major that looks similar on screen. Step five, voice the chords instead of leaving them in root position, and notice that this is free in note data: the notes move up or down by a value and the sound regenerates. Step six, use velocity rather than a mixer fader when you want a chord to sit back, because velocity belongs to the note and travels with it while a track level applies to everything on the track. Step seven, decide what kind of file you are making. If you export a .mid file, the manual states that .mid saves step-sequencer and piano-roll note data to a standard MIDI file and that MIDI is not an audio format, so nothing will be heard without an instrument; if you export audio, the manual lists .wav, .mp3, .ogg, .flac and .m4a as formats that save an audio mix of the project. Step eight, put a number on the difference in scale. A 30-second stereo audio file at 16 bits and 44,100 samples per second is 30 times 44,100 times 2 channels times 2 bytes, which is 5,292,000 bytes or about 5.05 MB, while the same thirty seconds as note data is a few values per note (computed). The grid that governs those values is worth knowing too: at 120 beats per minute a sixteenth note lasts 0.125 s, which at 44,100 samples per second is 5,512.5 samples, and at 128 beats per minute a sixteenth lasts about 0.117 s, roughly 5,168 samples (computed).
lessons.question: A learner finishes a sixteen-bar keyboard part, exports it as a .mid file and sends it to a friend, who reports that the file makes no sound anywhere it is opened. The same learner then wants to correct one wrong note in the chord in bar nine. Using the export documentation and the piano roll documentation, which pair of statements is accurate?
lessons.answer: The .mid file contains note data rather than sound, and the manual states outright that MIDI is not an audio format, so it stays silent until an instrument plays it; and because the part is note data, the wrong note is a value that can be changed in the piano roll rather than a performance that must be re-recorded
lessons.distractor: The .mid file should have played because MIDI is a compressed audio format that needs the matching codec installed; and the wrong note must be re-recorded because a finished part cannot be edited after export
lessons.correction: The export documentation lists .wav, .mp3, .ogg, .flac and .m4a as audio formats that save an audio mix of the project, and lists MIDI separately: .mid saves step-sequencer and piano-roll note data to a standard MIDI file, and the same page states that MIDI is not an audio format. Note data needs an instrument or a synthesiser to become sound, which is the same point the MIDI Out page makes when it says that MIDI Out does not make any sound of its own. The edit is then trivial rather than merely possible: the piano roll documentation says note data can be entered manually or recorded from live MIDI controllers and then edited to fix mistakes or make changes, so a single note is a value to correct, while the same note inside a recorded waveform would have to be sliced or re-performed.

depth.definitions: MIDI is a control and note-message protocol, not an audio format; note data is information about which notes occur, at what time, with what velocity and duration. Audio is a recorded waveform of sound. The piano roll is the note editor, and the Playlist is the arrangement window. A pattern is a block of note and automation data. Velocity is per-note data describing how hard the note is struck, distinct from a mixer track's level. The chord stamp tool places a chord of a chosen type at a clicked pitch and time. The Chord Progression Tool generates progressions and can snap the piano roll to a scale and root. Quantisation aligns events to a grid, whose resolution is set by the snap settings. Export means rendering or saving; a standard MIDI file contains note data rather than audio. Prerequisites: the recording-medium distinction from lesson 36, quantisation from lesson 38, the practice and error-budget habits of lesson 65, and the analysis method of lesson 75.
depth.mechanism: Note data is cheaper to work with because a note is a small set of parameters, and changing a parameter regenerates the sound rather than editing a copy of the sound. That is why the piano roll can offer tools like chord stamping, scale snapping and per-note velocity: each one writes values. Recorded audio has no such structure, so the operations available are waveform operations such as cutting, fading and pitch processing, and each of them changes the sound as well as the pitch. Three limits belong with this. First, a generator is not an analyst: the Chord Progression Tool's own documentation presents it as a way of getting valid chords in sequence, and validity is not the same as function, so a plausible loop may contain no structural dominant at all. Second, scale snapping changes notes that fall outside the chosen scale, which can conceal a wrong decision instead of correcting it, since a wrongly chosen chord tone will be quietly moved to a legal pitch. Third, if you drive external hardware from the project you also have to decide how that sound reaches the render, because note data sent to an external device is not captured until its audio is recorded into the project, which the MIDI Out page describes explicitly.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two routes to the same bar of D7 in C major. On the first route the learner stamps a chord at the seventh bar and accepts what appears, then discovers later that the tool produced D minor because the scale snapping was following the home key; the bar is legal, diatonic and structurally the wrong chord. On the second route the learner types four notes - D, F sharp, A and C - checks that F sharp is the raised note that identifies the chord as V7/V, and tells the tool to leave the bar alone. The second route costs thirty seconds and preserves the analysis. A second contrast concerns the same performance captured two ways: the identical keyboard chord recorded as Notes becomes a set of editable values that can be transposed, re-voiced, lengthened and re-timed, while the same chord recorded as Audio becomes a waveform whose timing can only be changed by cutting and moving fragments. A third contrast is between the two ways of making a chord quieter. Reducing the note velocities makes those notes softer wherever they appear and is part of the musical material; reducing the mixer level makes the whole track softer, which is a mix decision. Both are legitimate and they are not interchangeable.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is expecting sound from a file that contains data, which produces the exact complaint in this lesson's question: a .mid file that is silent because no instrument is attached to it. The diagnostic is to ask whether the file has an instrument or a waveform inside it; if it has neither, it is instructions. A second mistake is trusting a generator's output as an analysis, which inverts the order of this whole level: decide the function first, then let a tool help you enter it. A third is using scale snapping to repair a wrong note, which hides the error by moving it to a nearby legal pitch, so the diagnostic question is whether the note that was corrected was a typing mistake or a wrong chord choice. A fourth is conflating velocity with volume, which matters when you later change instruments: velocity is carried by the note and travels with the part, whereas a track level does not, so a part balanced only by a fader can change character completely on a different sound.
depth.application: Task, one session of 25 to 30 minutes at a low monitoring level, with a written analysis produced first and the project built afterwards. Choose eight bars from the unit one work. Write the function under every chord before opening the project. Then build the progression in the piano roll as note data, checking every chromatic chord by name rather than by ear alone, voice the chords in a small range instead of leaving them in root position, and use velocity for any note that needs to sit back. Finally, export two files: a standard MIDI file and an audio file of the same bars, and write one sentence for each saying what it contains and why. Model response: eight bars of C, A minor, D7, G7, F, F minor, C, G7 analysed as I, vi, V7/V, V7, IV, iv by mixture, I, V7; the D7 was typed rather than stamped because a stamped chord could have come out diatonic; F minor was confirmed by its A flat; voicings were kept inside an octave so the parts do not mask each other; the .mid file contains note data and would be silent without an instrument, and the audio file contains the sound as rendered. Self-review rubric: one point for functions written before the project was opened, one for each chromatic chord justified by naming its identifying note, one for a voicing decision that reduces register overlap, one for an accurate sentence about what each exported file contains. Keep monitoring low with the level set once, and treat ringing ears after a session as a signal to reduce the level rather than to continue.
depth.summary: A project stores two different kinds of object, and knowing which one you are handling decides what is cheap. Note data is a manageable set of values that can be transposed, re-voiced and re-timed, which is why the piano roll is the natural home for analysed harmony; audio is sound, and the operations available on it are different in kind rather than merely more expensive. Neither is better, and the skill is choosing deliberately at the moment of capture.

visual.title: Two kinds of object, two sets of operations - reasoning sequence
visual.description: The same bar of harmony held as note data and as a waveform, and the different operations each one permits.
steps: Decide the function before entering anything: bar seven is V7/V, so it must contain the raised note F sharp.
Enter it as note data in the piano roll, where four notes are four values and the D7 can be checked by naming its notes.

lessons.title: Put the key change in the project: a pivot on paper, a chord in your hands, a boundary in the Playlist
lessons.explanation: A modulation is not finished when it has been analysed; it has to be placed, and placing it well is mostly a matter of choosing where in the form it happens. Open Music Theory describes two routes in: the abrupt route, where the composer goes directly to the new key, which is often called a direct modulation and also a phrase modulation because it tends to occur at phrase boundaries and is recognised in analysis simply by labelling the new key and continuing; and the pivot route, which is subtler because a single chord belongs to both keys and carries the listener across. A project gives you both, and it also gives you something the theory chapters do not: seconds on a timeline. If a key change lands at the start of a sixteen-bar section in a thirty-two-bar form at 96 beats per minute, the change arrives at exactly 40.0 s into the piece, because each bar is 2.5 s and sixteen bars occupy 40.0 s (computed). Placing that boundary deliberately is most of the practical skill, and the structure vocabulary from the software manual supports it: a common pop layout is an intro of four bars, verses and choruses of eight or sixteen bars, a bridge of four or eight, repeated choruses and an outro of four, so the natural places to change key are the start of a repeated section or the start of the final chorus. Then comes the part that depends on lesson 78. If your parts are note data, transposing a section up a whole tone means adding two semitones to every pitch value, which is exact, reversible and free of artefacts. If a part is recorded audio, the same whole tone means processing a waveform rather than changing a number, and processing changes the sound as well as the pitch, so the two kinds of material have to be planned differently. There is also a cheaper route to a change of centre that is worth knowing before reaching for transposition: moving from a major key to its relative minor, or back, keeps the same collection, so nothing has to be transposed at all and only the harmonic centre and the emphasis change. Finally, an honest word about keys in popular music: the chapter on fragile, absent and emergent tonics exists because pop songs frequently do not have one unambiguous tonic, so a key change in this repertoire may be deliberately ambiguous, and the analysis should report that rather than forcing a single answer.
lessons.example: Plan and build a key change in three places at once, because that is the whole task. Step one, on paper: take a two-section sketch, sixteen bars in C major followed by sixteen bars in D major, and decide the route. The pivot route would use G, which is I in C and IV in D, as the shared chord, so the last bar of section one becomes the pivot and is written twice, once as I and once as IV. The direct route would end section one on a clear cadence in C and begin section two on D with no shared chord. Write the Roman numerals for both and choose one. Step two, in the hands: play the last four bars of section one into the first four bars of section two at 92 beats per minute, where a bar is 2.609 s and the eight bars you are playing span 20.87 s (computed). Listen for whether the change sounds announced or smuggled. Step three, in the project: put section two on its own place in the arrangement so the boundary is visible, and check the timeline arithmetic rather than guessing it. At 92 beats per minute a sixteen-bar section lasts 41.739 s, so the change lands at 41.739 s, and at 96 beats per minute a sixteen-bar section lasts 40.0 s, so the change lands at 40.0 s (computed). Step four, transpose the note data exactly. Raising every pitch value by two semitones is a whole tone, which is 200 cents, and because the change is applied to values rather than to a waveform it can be undone without any loss. Step five, treat the audio part differently and decide honestly what to do with it: re-record it in the new key, leave it out of the transposed section, or process it and accept the change in its sound. Step six, check the whole thing by ear at a moderate level and write down where the change actually becomes audible to you, which is often a bar or two later than the boundary you planned. Step seven, consider the relative-minor route before committing: keeping the collection and moving the centre from C major to A minor changes nothing in the pitch data at all, so if the musical goal is a change of mood rather than a change of range, it is the cheapest option available.
lessons.question: A producer wants to lift the final chorus by a whole tone. The project contains one chord part entered as note data and one recorded guitar part. Using the theory of modulation and the difference between note data and sound, which statement is accurate?
lessons.answer: Placing the change at the start of the repeated section fits how direct modulations usually work, the note data can be transposed exactly by two semitones per pitch value, and the recorded guitar is a waveform, so raising its pitch is processing sound rather than changing a value and has to be decided separately
lessons.distractor: Both parts transpose identically because a whole tone is two semitones either way, and the change can be placed anywhere inside the chorus since listeners adjust to a new key within a bar
lessons.correction: The two parts are different kinds of object, which the manual's distinction makes explicit when it states that .mid saves note data and that MIDI is not an audio format: a pitch in note data is a value, so transposing it is exact and reversible, while a pitch in recorded sound is a property of a waveform, so changing it means processing the audio and the result changes more than the pitch. The placement question is theoretical rather than technical: direct modulations are described as tending to occur at phrase boundaries, and section starts are the boundaries listeners use, which is why the change belongs at the top of the repeated section rather than inside it.

depth.definitions: A modulation is a longer-term change of tonic. A direct or phrase modulation moves straight to the new key, typically at a phrase or section boundary. A pivot chord modulation crosses through a chord diatonic in both keys. Closely related keys have signatures one degree sharper or flatter, and there are five such keys for any major or minor key. A whole tone is two semitones, which is 200 cents. Transposition of note data adds a constant interval to pitch values; pitch processing of audio changes a waveform. A section is a formal block; in the software it is placed in the arrangement window, called the Playlist. Prerequisites: modulation and pivot choice from lesson 72, cadences as confirmation from lesson 74, and the note-data and audio distinction from lesson 78.
depth.mechanism: A key change sounds convincing for two reasons that can be engineered separately. The first is preparation: a pivot chord, or a cadence in the old key followed by a clear tonic in the new one, gives the listener a route rather than a jump, and the sources recommend pivots that are predominant in both keys because the dominant then arrives in both readings. The second is placement: listeners segment music at boundaries marked by several changes at once, so a change of key at a section start is absorbed as part of the new section's identity, while the same change inside a phrase sounds like an error. Two limits belong with this. Direct modulations are entirely normal in this repertoire, so the absence of a pivot is not a fault, it is a different device. And popular music does not always have a stable tonic to modulate away from: the chapter on fragile, absent and emergent tonics exists precisely because some songs establish their centre late, ambiguously, or by implication, so an arrangement decision may be about making a centre clearer rather than about moving it.
depth.secondExample: Contrast three routes to the same musical goal, which is a final section that feels higher. Route one is the direct modulation: end section one with an authentic cadence and start section two a whole tone higher, which is simple, audibly a new event, and requires every melodic part to be re-voiced by two semitones. Route two is the pivot modulation: place a shared chord in the final bar of section one, so the same chord is heard as the old tonic and then reinterpreted as the subdominant of the new key, which is smooth and depends entirely on that chord being diatonic in both keys - in the C to D case, G, which is I in C and IV in D. Route three changes the centre without changing the notes: move from C major to A minor, which shares the whole collection, so nothing in the pitch data moves and only the emphasis and the harmony change. Contrast the three for effort: route one costs a transposition of every data part; route two costs one added chord and no transposition if the new key reuses the same pitch material; route three costs nothing at all in the data. A second contrast concerns the same change made in two media. Applying it to note data is a values operation that can be undone; applying it to a recorded guitar means either re-recording, dropping the part, or processing the audio, each with a different cost to the sound.
depth.mistake: The most common mistake is placing the change inside a phrase rather than at a boundary, where the same harmonic motion that would sound deliberate at a section start sounds like a mistake in the middle of one. The diagnostic is to move the boundary and listen twice, and then to write down which version a listener could describe. A second mistake is assuming that every part can be transposed the same way, which confuses note data with sound and leads to processing a recorded part and then wondering why its character changed. A third is assuming a modulation must be smooth; direct or phrase modulations are an ordinary device in this repertoire, and a chorus that simply arrives two semitones higher is neither a mistake nor an unsophisticated one. A fourth is expecting the project's key or scale settings to do the transposition for you: the scale and root setting in the piano roll governs snapping, highlighting and shading, which is a tool setting rather than a statement about the piece, and it will not move existing pitches by itself.
depth.application: Task in two sittings of no more than 25 minutes each, at a low monitoring level with the level set once. Sitting one, planning: choose two sixteen-bar sections and decide the key of each; write the Roman numerals for the last four bars of section one and the first four of section two; then write the same four bars twice, once as a direct modulation and once with a pivot chord, and mark which chords are data parts and which are recorded. Sitting two, building and checking: place section two at its own boundary in the arrangement, transpose the data parts exactly if the new key requires it, decide what happens to any audio part and write the reason down, then compute and state where the change occurs in seconds at your tempo. Model response for sixteen bars at 92 beats per minute: bar length 2.609 s, section length 41.739 s, so the change lands at 41.739 s; pivot chosen was G, functioning as I in the old key and IV in the new; the keyboard chord part was transposed by two semitones as data; the recorded guitar was dropped from the second section and will be re-recorded rather than processed, because processing would change its sound; the change is audible to me about one bar after the boundary. Self-review rubric: one point for both routes written in Roman numerals before building, one for a boundary placed where the form changes section, one for treating data and audio parts by different methods and saying why, one for the timeline computed in seconds rather than estimated. Set the monitor level once and leave it alone, keep each sitting under half an hour, and reduce the level if your ears ring afterwards.
depth.summary: A key change is a decision made in three media at once: it is an analysis on paper, a set of pitches in the hands, and a boundary on a timeline. Choosing the route, placing it at a boundary, and separating what can be transposed as data from what has to be handled as sound is the whole of the practical work, and the relative-minor route is the cheapest change of centre available when the pitch material does not need to move at all.

readings.note: Read the material on Patterns, Audio Clips and Automation Clips, the Playlist Snap entry, and the Bouncing to Audio or Freezing section. Snap is described as determining how clips move and how quantisation aligns events relative to the grid, which is how you guarantee that a section boundary lands on a bar line. The consolidation and freezing tools are how playlist material becomes a rendered file, which is the next step after the boundary is placed. Read it for the mechanics of the boundary rather than for creative guidance.

readings.title: [119] Open Music Theory - Fragile, Absent, and Emergent Tonics
readings.note: Read the chapter opening and the discussion of how a tonic can be established late, weakly or implicitly in popular music. It is the reason this lesson insists that a key change in this repertoire be reported honestly, including cases where the analysis cannot settle on one tonic, rather than forcing every arrangement into a single key. Access caveat verified during authoring: HTTP 403 to a plain command-line fetch, HTTP 200 to a browser user agent.

readings.title: [120] Open Music Theory - Extended Tonicization and Modulation to Closely Related Keys, section Direct modulations
readings.note: This is the second reading from this chapter in the level, and here read only the Direct modulations section. It explains that abrupt modulations are called direct modulations, that they are also called phrase modulations because they tend to occur at phrase boundaries, and that recognising one in analysis means labelling the new key and continuing with the analysis. That is the justification for placing a key change at the start of a repeated section in an arrangement. Access caveat as above: browser user agent required.

visual.title: A key change built on paper, in the hands and on the timeline - reasoning sequence
visual.description: Two routes written as Roman numerals, one chosen and placed at a section boundary, then computed in seconds on the arrangement.
steps: Write both routes before choosing: a direct modulation starting section two a whole tone higher, and a pivot modulation with a shared chord at the end of section one.
Check the pivot is genuinely diatonic in both keys: G is I in C major and IV in D major, so it can carry the listener across.
Place the change at a section boundary, since direct modulations tend to occur at phrase boundaries and listeners segment music there.
Compute the boundary instead of estimating it: sixteen bars at 92 beats per minute is 41.739 s, and at 96 beats per minute it is 40.0 s.

Treat the media differently: add two semitones to every pitch value in note data, and decide separately what to do with any recorded audio, since processing a waveform changes its sound as well as its pitch.

lessons.title: Capstone: two sections, one proven key change, a rendered file and an honest note
lessons.explanation: This capstone asks for something narrower than a finished song and stricter than a sketch: two sections, at least one chromatic event you can name, a key change you can prove, a rendered audio file, and a short written note that is accurate about what the file contains. The proof standard is not negotiable, because it comes straight from the theory: a modulation to a new key requires an eventual cadence to confirm that new key, so a second section that merely begins on a new chord is a tonicization at best and an unconfirmed assertion at worst. Naming the chromatic events is the second half of the standard. For every chromatic chord in your piece you should be able to say whether it is an applied chord or a mixture chord, and to justify the answer: an applied chord shares its root with a diatonic chord and has been altered so that it acts as a dominant or leading-tone chord of another degree, while mixture borrows a chord from the parallel mode of the same tonic. The third part of the standard is delivery, and the software manual is precise about it. Audio formats such as .wav, .mp3, .ogg, .flac and .m4a save an audio mix of the project, while .mid saves note data and the manual states that MIDI is not an audio format; the Master mixer track is rendered by default, so anything not routed to it is left out of the file; and the length of a render is decided by a stated hierarchy of time selection, the last time marker beyond the last bar containing data, the end of the last bar containing data, and the tail setting. Those details are exactly the kind of thing that makes an otherwise finished piece arrive incomplete. The fourth part is monitoring, and it is a safety requirement rather than a preference. Published hearing-conservation guidance for musicians states that the extent of damage is predicted by how loud and how long you are listening, not by what device you listen through, and it notes that loudness plus duration equals damage, with 85 decibels named as a standard reference level for headphone limiting. Set the monitor level once, keep it moderate, and treat ringing ears after a session as evidence that the level was too high rather than as a normal cost of working.
lessons.example: Here is the capstone specification with every figure computed rather than estimated. Build two sixteen-bar sections at 92 beats per minute, so a beat is 0.652 s, a bar is 2.609 s, each section is 41.739 s and the total is 83.478 s (computed). Section one is in C major and contains at least one chromatic chord you can name; a suitable choice is the doo-wop pattern C, A minor, F, G, with D7 inserted before the G in the second half so the passage contains V7/V. Section two is in D major and is reached by a pivot. Step one, write the analysis on paper first: section one as I, vi, IV, V7/V, V7, and the pivot G functioning as I in C major and IV in D major at the join. Step two, prove the new key. Section two must contain a cadence in D major; a section that begins on D and never cadences in D has not been shown to be in D at all. Step three, decide the medium of every part and write it down, because the note in the delivery has to say which parts are note data and which are recorded sound, and because the two require different handling when the key changes. Step four, set levels once, with headroom, and leave them alone. Step five, render the audio file: 83.478 s at 44,100 samples per second, two channels and two bytes per sample is 83.478 times 44,100 times 2 times 2, which is 14,725,565 bytes, or about 14.04 MB (computed). Step six, check the render against the manual's length hierarchy rather than trusting it: if you made a time selection, the render is that selection; otherwise it runs to the last time marker beyond the last bar with data, or to the end of the last bar with data, plus the tail. If a track is missing, check whether it is routed to the Master mixer track, because that is what is rendered by default. Step seven, listen on a second system at a moderate level and note the first thing that sounds wrong. Step eight, write the delivery note in five sentences: the two keys; the cadence that proves the second one; each chromatic chord and whether it is applied or mixture; which parts are note data and which are audio, and anything that was edited; and the single weakest moment and what you would do about it. A model note in that form reads: the piece is two sixteen-bar sections at 92 beats per minute, C major then D major, joined by G as a pivot; D major is confirmed by an authentic cadence at bar thirty-two; the chromatic chords are D7 as V7/V in section one and F natural as the third of the mixture chord in bar twelve; the chord part is note data and the bass line is recorded audio, with one cut at the section boundary; the weakest moment is the second bar of the new key, and I would give it a clearer tonic emphasis before releasing the file.
lessons.question: A learner submits the capstone project: a 16-bit stereo WAV at 44.1 kHz lasting 83.478 s, a claim that the piece modulates to D major because the second section starts on a D chord, and a description of the keyboard part as a recording of the performance. Using the export documentation and this level's requirements, what has to be corrected?
lessons.answer: The claim needs a cadence in D major rather than merely a section beginning on D, the keyboard part must be described as note data rather than as a recording, and the file size for 83.478 s of 16-bit stereo at 44.1 kHz is about 14.04 MB (computed)
lessons.distractor: Neither the claim nor the description needs changing, because a section that begins on D establishes D major and because a rendered audio file is by definition a recording of the performance captured
lessons.correction: Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom states that a modulation to a new key requires an eventual cadence to confirm that new key, so a section that begins on D without a cadence in D has not demonstrated a modulation; at best it is a tonicization of the new tonic, and the analyst should say so. The description is a separate factual error: the export documentation distinguishes the audio formats that save an audio mix from .mid, which saves step-sequencer and piano-roll note data, and it states that MIDI is not an audio format, and the same distinction holds inside the project, where a keyboard part captured as Notes is performance information rather than sound. The arithmetic checks the file claim: 83.478 times 44,100 times two channels times two bytes is 14,725,565 bytes, which is about 14.04 MB.

depth.definitions: A capstone is a bounded demonstration rather than a complete work. A delivery note is a short written statement accompanying a file that says what it contains and what it does not. Rendering or exporting turns a project into a file; the Master mixer track is rendered by default. Bit depth is the resolution of each sample, with 16-bit generally sufficient for distribution and 24 or 32-bit intended for archiving production material. Proof of modulation means a cadence in the new key. Note data is performance information; audio is recorded sound. A pivot chord is diatonic in both keys. Reference listening means judging a render on a system other than the one it was made on. Prerequisites: applied chords from lesson 71, cadences as confirmation from lessons 72 and 74, the analysis method of lesson 75, the note-data distinction of lesson 78, and the placement decisions of lesson 79.
depth.mechanism: The capstone is built on criteria rather than on taste, for a reason that has evidence behind it. Music practice research has found that how much time was spent was not the variable related to retention quality, while the proportion of correct executions was, which is the same logic applied to delivery: what is checked is what improves, so the note specifies what will be checked. Self-assessment has its own documented weakness, since learners' judgements of their own performances agree less with expert ratings and improve with experience, which is why the note asks for named criteria and a conceded weakness rather than a summary impression. Three limits belong with the deliverable. A render can be short, long or missing a track for reasons that have nothing to do with the performance, which is why the length hierarchy and the master routing are checked explicitly. A file is not proof of understanding, and a level like this is a bounded demonstration rather than professional competence. And an honest note that says a part was never recorded, or that a key change was not confirmed, is worth more than a claim that cannot be checked.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two submissions of the same music. The first delivers a file named final, asserts a modulation because the second half sounds higher, describes the keyboard part as a recording, and says nothing about what was edited. The second delivers the same music with a note stating the two keys, the cadence that proves the second one, the two chromatic chords with their functions, the medium of each part, the one edit made at the section boundary, and the weakest bar with a plan for it. Both submissions took the same playing time; only the second can be acted on by another musician, and only the second gives its author a record that shortens the next session. A second contrast concerns the proof itself: the same two sections can be made convincing either by ending section one with an authentic cadence in C and beginning section two on a clear D, which is a direct modulation at a boundary, or by carrying a shared G across the join as a pivot. The first needs a cadence in the new key to be defensible; the second additionally needs the pivot to be diatonic in both keys, which G is, since it is I in C and IV in D.
depth.mistake: The commonest failure is claiming more than the material shows, so a section that begins on a new chord is described as a modulation without a cadence to confirm it, or a part is described as recorded when it was captured as note data. The diagnostic is to read your own note and ask what evidence each sentence would need; a sentence that cannot be checked is a claim rather than a description. A second mistake is rendering and not listening, which misses both the length hierarchy and the master routing problems that make delivered files incomplete. A third is judging the render on the same system it was made on, at a level that was raised during the session and never returned, which reliably produces a mix that sounds wrong everywhere else. A fourth is finishing the level and describing it as mastery: a bounded demonstration with a proven key change shows that a method has been understood, and it does not establish professional competence.
depth.application: Capstone task, in three sittings of no more than 30 minutes each, with the monitor level set once and left moderate. Sitting one, plan and analyse: write the two keys, the pivot or the direct change, the cadence that will confirm the new key, and the name and function of every chromatic chord. Sitting two, build and play: enter or play the two sections, place the boundary in the arrangement, and warm up before any playing. Sitting three, render, listen and write: render the audio file, compute its expected size, check the render length against the manual's hierarchy, listen on one other system at a moderate level, and write the five-sentence note described in the example. Model response for the specification in this lesson: two sixteen-bar sections at 92 beats per minute, 41.739 s each and 83.478 s total; C major to D major with G as the pivot, D major confirmed by an authentic cadence at bar thirty-two; chromatic events are D7 as V7/V and an F natural in the mixture chord at bar twelve; chord part is note data, bass is recorded audio with one cut at the boundary; weakest moment is the first two bars of D major and the fix is to state the new tonic more plainly. Self-review rubric: one point for a key change proved by a cadence rather than asserted, one for every chromatic chord named as applied or mixture with a reason, one for an accurate statement about which parts are note data and which are audio, one for a file that exists, is the expected size, and contains every part you intended, one for a note that concedes something specific. Keep each sitting under 30 minutes, warm up before playing, and if your ears ring afterwards, lower the level before you continue rather than enduring it.
depth.summary: The capstone compresses the level into one habit: analyse before you build, prove what you claim, deliver something a listener can actually open, and describe it accurately, including its weaknesses. The method transfers to the next piece, to any session where somebody asks what key you are in and how you know, and to every file you hand to another musician.
