About Rendering states that the Master mixer track is rendered by default unless individual tracks are split, and that audio formats save an audio mix while .mid saves step-sequencer and piano-roll note data, with the explicit statement that MIDI is not an audio format. Render length gives the hierarchy of time selection, the last time marker beyond the last bar containing data, the end of the last bar containing data and the tail setting, which is what makes a bounce shorter or longer than expected. Output format gives the bit-depth guidance used here. Read it before rendering anything for delivery.

readings.title: [122] University of Iowa Head and Neck Protocols - Considerations and Tips for Hearing Conservation: Information for Musicians
readings.note: Read the opening and the Personal Listening Devices section. It states that the extent of damage is predicted by how loud and how long you listen rather than by which device is used, that high volume combined with long duration causes damage, and that monitoring tools and headphone limits are available, with 85 decibels given as a standard limit value in that context. This is public health guidance about hearing rather than a diagnosis of your hearing, and it is the basis for setting the monitor level once and keeping it moderate.

readings.title: [123] Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom (Robert Hutchinson) - Section 22.5 How to Recognize a Key After a Modulation
readings.note: Read the whole short section as a final checklist before writing the delivery note. It gives the cues for locating a new key: look for recurring accidentals and add them to the key signature, remember that lowered notes usually create the fourth degree and raised notes usually create the leading tone, that multiple raised notes should be read in key-signature order to find which is acting as the leading tone, and that accidentals which cancel out indicate tonicizations or chromatic non-chord tones rather than a new key. Those cues are what let you say, in one sentence, how you know which key the second section is in.

visual.title: The capstone as four checks in order - reasoning sequence
visual.description: Plan and analyse, prove the change, render what was intended, and describe the result accurately.
steps: Write the two keys and the join before building: C major to D major with G as a pivot that is I in the old key and IV in the new one.
Require a cadence in the new key, since a modulation is confirmed by an arrival rather than by a section that merely begins on a new chord.
Convert the form into time and into bytes: sixteen bars at 92 beats per minute is 41.739 s per section, 83.478 s in total, and about 14.04 MB as 16-bit stereo audio at 44.1 kHz (computed).

Check the render against the manual's rules before delivering it: the Master mixer track is rendered by default, and render length follows a stated hierarchy of selection, time marker, last bar with data and tail.
Listen once on another system at a moderate level, then write the five-sentence note, including one weakness and what you would change.

questions.prompt: A guitarist in C major plays D7 then G7 and finds the change sounds disconnected even though both chords are correct. Using guide tones and the construction of applied dominants, what single change is recommended, and what does it look like on the instrument?
questions.answer: Play only the guide tones of D7, F sharp on the fourth string at the fourth fret and C on the second string at the first fret, and move both down one semitone to F at the third fret and the open B string, which are the guide tones of G7
questions.distractor: Move both chords into the same inversion and add the root of each chord in the bass, so that the voices move in parallel and the progression sounds even
questions.correction: Guide tones are the third and the seventh of a chord, and in a fifth progression they move by step; that is why the smallest version of this change is not a pair of chords but a pair of voices. In D7 the guide tones are F sharp and C, and in G7 they are B and F, so F sharp falls a semitone to F and C falls a semitone to B, with both voices moving in the same direction and the hand shape unchanged. Playing root-position block chords in parallel motion removes the two semitone motions that make the resolution sound intended, which is why the progression sounds disconnected even though the harmony is correct.

questions.prompt: A learner has written a four-bar passage in D Aeolian with the chords D minor and G minor, and wants the same notes to sound Dorian instead. On the instrument and in the harmony, what is the smallest change that achieves it, and what is the evidence that it worked?
questions.answer: Raise the sixth degree from B flat to B natural, which on the fourth string is moving from fret 8 to fret 9, and change the accompanying chord from G minor to G major so the progression becomes the Dorian shuttle of i to IV
questions.distractor: Raise the fourth degree and add a C sharp, because Dorian is major with a lowered seventh and the fourth is the note that carries the mode
questions.correction: Dorian is natural minor with a raised sixth, so the one note that changes is the sixth degree: B flat becomes B natural, which on the D string is fret 8 moving to fret 9, a single fret. Raising the fourth degree and lowering the seventh describes Mixolydian and produces the wrong mode. The chord change matters as much as the note: the modal schema literature names the Dorian shuttle as i to IV, which in D is D minor to G major, so the G major is what makes the raised sixth audible as a mode rather than as an accident, while the original G minor kept the passage in Aeolian.

questions.prompt: A learner built an eight-bar keyboard chord part, then wants three things: to change one wrong note in a chord, to move the whole part up a whole tone, and to try a completely different instrument sound. The part was captured from the keyboard, and a recorded bass guitar sits underneath it. Which material can do all three, and what does the manual say about the file that the recorded part will not appear in as data?
questions.answer: The keyboard part can do all three because it is note data, whose pitches are values that can be edited, transposed by two semitones and re-voiced with any instrument; the recorded bass is a waveform, and .mid saves note data with the manual stating that MIDI is not an audio format, so the bass cannot be carried that way
questions.distractor: Both parts can do all three because a whole tone is two semitones whether the material is data or sound, and a .mid file carries the complete mix so both parts travel in it
questions.correction: The manual's export page lists audio formats that save an audio mix and lists .mid separately as saving step-sequencer and piano-roll note data, adding that MIDI is not an audio format, so a .mid file carries instructions rather than sound. Note data is a set of values, so a wrong note is corrected by changing a value, a transposition adds a constant interval to every pitch, and the instrument can be swapped because the sound is generated later. None of those operations applies to a recorded waveform, which contains the performance as sound; changing its pitch is processing the audio rather than changing a number, and it cannot be re-voiced at all.

questions.prompt: A producer finishing a thirty-two-bar arrangement at 96 beats per minute wants the final sixteen-bar section a whole tone higher, reached through a shared chord. Where does the change fall in seconds, which chord can carry it from C major to D major, and what has to be decided about any recorded audio in the transposed section?
questions.answer: The change falls at 40.0 s, G can carry it because it is I in C major and IV in D major, and any recorded audio part must be decided separately, since raising its pitch is processing sound rather than changing a data value
questions.distractor: The change falls at 80.0 s because the whole form is thirty-two bars, and F can carry it because the subdominant is shared between the two keys, with recorded audio transposed in the same operation as the data
questions.correction: At 96 beats per minute a beat is 0.625 s, so a bar is 2.5 s and the final sixteen-bar section begins at the sixteenth bar, which is 16 times 2.5 s, or 40.0 s; 80.0 s is the end of the complete thirty-two-bar form. G is diatonic in both keys, as I in C major and IV in D major, which is the combination the pivot literature prefers, while F is IV in C and therefore not shared. Placing the change at a section boundary follows the description of direct modulations as tending to occur at phrase boundaries. The last decision is a medium decision: note data transposes exactly by adding two semitones to each pitch value, whereas recorded audio has to be re-recorded, dropped or processed, and processing alters the sound as well as the pitch.

questions.prompt: A learner reports that a session was cut short after twenty minutes with two errors late in the passage, that the monitor level had to be raised to hear the inner part, and that the next session will therefore be longer and louder to make up for it. Which response is consistent with the practice and safety material in this level?
questions.answer: Shorten and structure the work instead: isolate the smallest version of the passage, climb a tempo ladder with a written error count, warm up first, and set the monitor level once at a moderate setting rather than raising it
questions.distractor: Extend the next session and raise the level, because total practice time is what determines retention and a louder monitor reveals detail that quieter listening masks
questions.correction: The recorded evidence runs the other way on both counts. In the study of pianists learning a difficult passage, retention quality was not significantly related to practice time, total trials or complete trials, while the percentage of trials performed correctly was, so the errors late in the passage are the informative part of the report and the fix is to slow down and shrink the material. On the hearing side, published conservation guidance for musicians states that the extent of damage is predicted by how loud and how long you listen rather than by the device, and separately, the survey of guitar practice injuries found that failure to warm up was the only variable statistically associated with increased risk, which supports a warm-up before the work rather than a longer session.

questions.prompt: A rehearsal chart in G major reads G, E minor, A7, D7, G, one chord per bar, at 104 beats per minute. A player asks which chords leave the key, what each should be called, and how long the progression lasts. Computed from that tempo, which answer is correct?
questions.answer: A7 is V7/V and D7 is V7, so only A7 leaves the key, and five bars at 104 beats per minute last 11.538 s
questions.distractor: Both A7 and D7 leave the key, since each contains a note foreign to G major, and five bars at 104 beats per minute last 2.308 s
questions.correction: The diatonic triads of G major are G, A minor, B minor, C, D, E minor and F sharp diminished, so D7 is diatonic in root and quality: D major is V and adding the seventh makes V7, which is the home dominant rather than an applied chord. A7 is not diatonic, because the second degree of G major is A minor; the quality test gives major-minor seventh, a perfect fifth below A is D, and D is the root of V, so A7 is V7/V. At 104 beats per minute a beat is 60 divided by 104, which is 0.577 s, so a 4/4 bar is 2.308 s and five bars are 11.538 s, not 2.308 s, which is the duration of a single bar.

questions.prompt: A composer wants to move from G major to D major. Asked which chords are shared and which should be the pivot, a student answers that all seven diatonic triads are available and that D should be the pivot because it is the tonic of the new key. What is the accurate correction, including the count of shared triads?
questions.answer: Only four of the seven triads are diatonic in both keys, namely G, B minor, D and E minor, which is 57.1 per cent; E minor is the strongest pivot because it is vi in the old key and ii in the new one, while D is the pairing the sources warn against
questions.distractor: All seven triads are shared because the two keys differ by one sharp, and D is the ideal pivot because a chord that becomes the tonic makes the new key clear immediately
questions.correction: A diatonic common chord modulation requires the pivot to be diatonic in both keys with the same root and the same quality, and comparing the two lists shows that only G, B minor, D and E minor satisfy that, which is four of seven, about 57.1 per cent. The pivot choice is then a question of function: the recommended best case is a chord that is predominant in both keys, which E minor is, being vi in G and ii in D. D is V in the old key and I in the new one, the combination described as potentially abrupt and unconvincing, so it is the weakest of the four candidates rather than the strongest, despite becoming the new tonic.

questions.prompt: A learner writes a passage that uses only the white keys, returns constantly to A, and calls it A Dorian; a second passage uses only white keys, returns constantly to C, and is called C Ionian. A third passage in A Dorian then requires an F sharp, which the learner believes is an error. Using the modal definitions and the colour-note idea, which reading is correct?
questions.answer: The first is A Aeolian and the second is C Ionian since both read the same collection from different centres, and A Dorian genuinely requires F sharp because Dorian raises the sixth degree relative to natural minor
questions.distractor: The first is A Dorian and the second is C Lydian because the same collection read from a different note produces the mode's name, and the F sharp in the third passage is an error since Dorian never leaves the collection
questions.correction: Within the white-note collection, Ionian starts on C, Dorian on D, Phrygian on E, Lydian on F, Mixolydian on G and Aeolian on A; so white keys centred on A are Aeolian, which is identical to natural minor and has no raised leading tone, while white keys centred on C are Ionian, which is identical to major. Lydian is not involved because nothing in the second passage raises the fourth degree. The two descriptions of mode are both standard and both apply: relatively, a mode is a collection read from a particular final, and in parallel terms it is a major or minor scale with one degree inflected. A Dorian is therefore natural minor with a raised sixth, which in A requires F sharp, and the analysis literature notes both that modes can be transposed and that modal music may even contain pitches outside the collection.

questions.prompt: Three four-bar phrases in C major end as follows: the first with G7 followed by C, C in the bass and the tonic in the soprano; the second with G7 followed by C in first inversion with the third in the soprano; the third with G7 followed by A minor. A learner labels all three as imperfect authentic cadences. What is the accurate set of labels and the reasoning?
questions.answer: The first is a perfect authentic cadence, the second an imperfect authentic cadence and the third a deceptive cadence, whose more accurate description is that V moved to not-I
questions.distractor: The first is a plagal cadence because the tonic is in the bass and the soprano, the second is a half cadence because it does not reach root position, and the third is an imperfect authentic cadence because the final chord is minor
questions.correction: An authentic cadence is V to I, perfect when both harmonies are in root position and the tonic scale degree is in the soprano over tonic, and imperfect when either condition fails; the first phrase meets both conditions and the second meets neither, so both remain authentic cadences of different strength. A plagal cadence requires IV to I and a half cadence requires a phrase ending on V, so neither description fits a phrase that ends on the tonic in any inversion. The third phrase does not end on the tonic at all, which makes it a deceptive cadence, and the sources note that because a deceptive cadence means V did not go to I, the description V to not-I is technically more accurate than V to vi, which is merely the most common realisation.

questions.prompt: A learner analyses a sixteen-bar section at 96 beats per minute by naming chords from left to right, reaching bar nine before the labels stop making sense, having meanwhile labelled every chromatic chord by its root degree. Using the harmonic-analysis method and the applied-chord test, what is the correct procedure and what does the failure at bar nine indicate?
questions.answer: Phrase endings and cadences should have been identified before any chord was named, since cadences establish keys; the breakdown at bar nine most likely marks a change of key or an extended tonicization, and the chromatic chords should have been tested by quality and by the fifth below their roots rather than named by degree
questions.distractor: Chord naming from left to right is the correct procedure for a sixteen-bar section, and the breakdown indicates that the section is in two keys simultaneously, which is why a single set of labels cannot be applied
questions.correction: The documented method is ordered: identify phrase endings by listening, analyse the cadence at each ending, back up from the cadence to find the strong predominant, and only then analyse from the beginning, assigning one set of tonic beginning, predominant, dominant and tonic ending labels per phrase. That order locates key changes, because a cadence is what establishes a new tonic. Naming chromatic chords by root degree fails the quality test, since a chromatic chord's identity depends on being a major or major-minor-seventh chord whose root sits a perfect fifth above a diatonic root; a sixteen-bar section in two keys at once is not a coherent analysis, whereas a section with a modulation is a normal one.

questions.prompt: A learner in the key of F major is told to play the applied dominant before the B flat chord. She assumes a barre chord high on the neck is required and reports that the change tires her hand after two minutes. Using the construction of applied chords, the guide-tone reduction and the practice-injury material, what is the accurate response?
questions.answer: The chord is F7, the F shape with one finger moved from the fourth string third fret to the first fret to add E flat, so no barre is needed; and tiring after two minutes calls for a warm-up, a relaxed setup and short bursts rather than more force
questions.distractor: The chord is a barre shape two frets above the existing F, because applied dominants are always outside the key and require movable shapes; the hand will strengthen with repetition so the discomfort can be worked through
questions.correction: In F major the chord before IV is V7/IV, which is the tonic turned into a dominant seventh: F7, spelled F, A, C, E flat. The lowered note, E flat, acts as the fourth degree of the chord being tonicized, which is B flat, and on the guitar it is the fourth string at the first fret, so the only movement is one finger crossing two frets within a shape already held. The fatigue point is separate: a survey of guitar players reported injury related to practice in 53 per cent of 105 respondents, calculated as one injury per 2,381 practice hours, and found failure to warm up was the only variable statistically associated with increased risk. Working through a tiring change strengthens nothing; adjusting the setup, warming up and keeping bursts short is what the evidence supports.

questions.prompt: A learner plays D Dorian on the keyboard using only white keys, then plays G Mixolydian, then claims that both modes are the white keys and that a mode is therefore a matter of where you start. Testing the claim against a transposition, which statement is accurate?
questions.answer: Both statements are true only when the tonic is D and G respectively; transposing the same modes shows the claim fails, since A Dorian requires F sharp and D Mixolydian requires F sharp, so a mode is a collection with a centre rather than a fixed set of white keys
questions.distractor: The claim is correct because every mode is a rotation of the same seven-note collection, so a mode is completely determined by its starting note and never acquires accidentals when transposed
questions.correction: The relative description of modes is that the white-note collection read from C, D, E, F, G and A gives Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian and Aeolian, and this is accurate for that specific collection. The parallel description is that each mode is a major or minor scale with one degree inflected, so Dorian is natural minor with a raised sixth and Mixolydian is major with a lowered seventh. The two descriptions coincide only for the white-note collection; transpose and they separate, because A Dorian, which is A natural minor with F raised to F sharp, uses one black key, and D Mixolydian uses F sharp as its lowered seventh against D major. A collection without a centre does not determine a mode, which is why the analysis literature offers a centre-finding heuristic and allows chromatic notes inside modal music.

questions.prompt: A learner types an eight-bar chord progression into the piano roll, records a guitar part over it, then exports both a .mid file and a WAV. A friend reports that the .mid file is silent, and the learner wants to know why one file is silent and how big the audio file should be for forty seconds of 16-bit stereo audio at 44.1 kHz. Which answer is correct?
questions.answer: The .mid file holds note data and the manual states that MIDI is not an audio format, so it needs an instrument to become sound, while forty seconds of 16-bit stereo audio at 44.1 kHz is 40 times 44,100 times 2 times 2 bytes, which is 7,056,000 bytes or about 6.73 MB
questions.distractor: The .mid file is silent because it stores the guitar audio with a codec the friend lacks, and forty seconds of 16-bit stereo audio at 44.1 kHz is about 3.36 MB because audio files store one channel of data
questions.correction: The export documentation lists .wav, .mp3, .ogg, .flac and .m4a as formats that save an audio mix and lists MIDI separately as saving step-sequencer and piano-roll note data, then states that MIDI is not an audio format; the same point appears in the MIDI Out documentation, which says MIDI Out does not make any sound of its own. So a silent .mid file is behaving exactly as documented, because nothing in it generates sound. The size arithmetic is 40 times 44,100 samples per second times two channels times two bytes, which is 7,056,000 bytes or about 6.73 MB, and halving the channel count would give half that figure rather than a quarter, since the bytes per sample and the sample rate are unchanged.

questions.prompt: A producer finishes a thirty-two-bar arrangement at 92 beats per minute and wants the final sixteen bars a whole tone higher, joining the sections with a shared chord. The melodic parts are note data and the rhythm guitar is recorded audio. Which plan is accurate about the boundary in seconds, the pivot, and the treatment of the two media?
questions.answer: The boundary falls at 41.739 s since a sixteen-bar section at 92 beats per minute lasts that long, G can serve as the pivot between C major and D major, the note data is transposed exactly by two semitones per pitch value, and the recorded guitar must be re-recorded, dropped or processed because its pitch is part of a waveform
questions.distractor: The boundary falls at 83.478 s because that is the length of the entire form, the pivot can be any chord because a shared chord is optional, and both media transpose identically since a whole tone is the same interval in each
questions.correction: At 92 beats per minute a beat is 60 divided by 92, which is 0.652 s, so a bar is 2.609 s and sixteen bars are 41.739 s; 83.478 s is the duration of the whole thirty-two-bar form, not of one section. G is diatonic in both C major and D major, being I in the first and IV in the second, so it can carry the listener across, and the pivot is the device that makes the change subtle rather than abrupt; a direct modulation without a pivot is also legitimate but must then be confirmed by a cadence in the new key. Note data and recorded audio are different objects, which is why the manual distinguishes a .mid file that saves note data from audio formats that save an audio mix and states that MIDI is not an audio format: a pitch in note data is a value and transposes exactly, while a pitch in a recording is a property of a waveform.

questions.prompt: Two learners each spend forty minutes on the same difficult four-bar passage. The first plays the whole passage at target tempo twelve times and makes four errors; the second isolates two beats, plays a tempo ladder from 60 to 100 beats per minute and requires nine clean runs out of ten before climbing. Both then practise the rest of the piece. Which description of the two sessions is supported by the practice evidence and by the safety material in this level?
questions.answer: The second approach is more likely to hold up, because the percentage of correct trials rather than the amount of time was what related to retention, and each rung's bar duration can be computed, ranging from 4.0 s at 60 beats per minute to 2.4 s at 100
questions.distractor: The first approach is more likely to hold up, because forty minutes of continuous repetition produces more total trials and the four errors are far too few to affect the stored version of the passage
questions.correction: In the study of pianists learning a difficult passage, retention quality showed no significant relationship with practice time, total trials or complete trials, while it did relate to the percentage of trials performed correctly and to the number of trials performed incorrectly; the first learner's four errors in twelve runs is a sixty-seven per cent correct rate, and each erroneous run is an additional stored version of the passage. The ladder timings check out arithmetically: at 60 beats per minute a 4/4 bar is 4.0 s and at 100 it is 2.4 s, a ratio of 1.667 between the slowest and fastest rungs. The study is small, seventeen pianists and one passage, so it is a hypothesis for your own written records rather than a law, and the safety material adds the warm-up and short-session habit on top of it.

questions.prompt: An eight-bar loop in C major runs C, A minor, F, G, C, A minor, D7, G7. A learner describes it as the doo-wop schema, calls the F minor in a later version a mistake, and labels the D7 as ii7. Which set of corrections is accurate?
questions.answer: The loop is the doo-wop pattern I, vi, IV, V, the D7 is V7/V because its root sits a perfect fifth above the diatonic root G, and an F minor chord is mixture borrowed from the parallel minor rather than an error
questions.distractor: The loop is the singer-songwriter schema vi, IV, I, V, the D7 is ii7 because its root is the second degree of the key, and an F minor chord is a modulation to F minor
questions.correction: The published schema list gives doo-wop as I, vi, IV, V and singer-songwriter as vi, IV, I, V; this loop begins on the tonic, so it is doo-wop, and the schema framing notes that such progressions recur cyclically and can be altered while remaining recognisable. Labelling by root degree fails the applied-chord test: D7 has major-minor seventh quality, and a perfect fifth below D is G, which is the root of V, so D7 is V7/V. An F minor chord contains A flat, which is not in C major, and it is borrowed from C minor, which is the definition of mode mixture; a single borrowed chord does not move the tonic, and a modulation would require a cadence in F minor to confirm it.

questions.prompt: A learner delivers the level capstone: two sixteen-bar sections at 92 beats per minute, C major then D major joined by a shared G, a keyboard part captured as note data and a recorded bass, an authentic cadence in the new key at the final bar, and a 16-bit stereo WAV at 44.1 kHz. During the session the monitor level was raised to hear an inner part and the learner reports ringing afterwards. Which statement about the package and the session is accurate?
questions.answer: The package is complete and defensible because the key change is confirmed by a cadence in the new key, the file for 83.478 s of 16-bit stereo audio at 44.1 kHz is about 14.04 MB, and the ringing means the monitor level was too high and must be reduced rather than tolerated
questions.distractor: The package is unsound because note data cannot be delivered alongside recorded audio, the file should be about 28.08 MB because both sections are stored twice, and ringing after a session is a normal consequence of monitoring at a level high enough to reveal detail
questions.correction: The delivery meets the standard in each respect. A modulation is proved by an eventual cadence in the new key, which the final bar supplies. A project may legitimately mix media: the manual distinguishes a .mid file that saves note data from audio formats that save an audio mix, and a rendered audio file captures whatever reaches the Master mixer track regardless of whether a part began as data or as sound. The size is 83.478 s times 44,100 samples per second times two channels times two bytes, which is 14,725,565 bytes, about 14.04 MB, and nothing is stored twice. On hearing, the conservation guidance states that damage is predicted by loudness and duration rather than by the device, and lists 85 decibels as a reference limit for headphone output, so persistent ringing is a signal to lower the level.
